title: Blocks, Pins, and Heavy Metal: Optimized Sample Preparation for Volume EM of Myelin in Mouse Central Nervous System.
abstract: Volume electron microscopy is a widely used technique to image complex tissue architecture at high resolution for 3D reconstruction. Originally developed for brain connectomics, this technology has proven important for other applications as well. Here we describe protocols established in our laboratories for the visualization of myelin in the mouse central nervous system. The main purpose of the protocol is the optimized preparation of small samples such as vibratome slices or optic nerves. We include possible substitutions for toxic chemicals in commonly used protocols. Tannic acid and neodymium acetate turned out suitable for the replacement of thiocarbohydrazide and uranyl acetate.

title: Immunohistochemical Analysis of Oligodendrocyte Lineage Cells and Myelin in Murine Central Nervous System.
abstract: White matter, composed of axons ensheathed in myelin produced by mature oligodendrocytes, is essential for the rapid and efficient transmission of electrical impulses throughout the nervous system. The development of oligodendrocytes follows a tightly regulated lineage progression, beginning with neural progenitor cells (NPCs) that differentiate into oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs). These OPCs undergo proliferation, migration, and ultimately terminal differentiation into mature, myelinating oligodendrocytes. Disruptions at any stage of this developmental cascade-whether in lineage specification, proliferation, migration, or maturation-can impair myelination and contribute to the pathophysiology of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). Therefore, identifying the precise stage at which oligodendrocyte lineage progression is altered is critical for elucidating the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying NDDs.

title: Metabolic Imaging of Optic Nerve Oligodendrocytes Following AAV-Mediated Sensor Delivery.
abstract: Oligodendrocytes are key regulators of white matter integrity, supporting rapid nerve conduction and sustaining axonal health. They engage in metabolic interactions with axons, yet their metabolic dynamics and specializations remain difficult to study in intact tissue. The optic nerve provides an accessible and well-structured white matter tract in which oligodendrocytes maintain their native association with axons and surrounding glia. Here, we present a protocol for targeted biosensor expression in oligodendrocytes of the optic nerve using intracerebroventricular injection of adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) at postnatal day 10 (P10). This approach enables imaging of oligodendrocyte metabolism in an intact 3D environment. As a use case, we demonstrate expression and application of a genetically encoded glucose sensor, allowing metabolic imaging to be combined with functional assays such as optic nerve electrophysiology. This method provides a flexible platform for studying oligodendrocyte physiology and metabolic adaptation in health and disease.

title: Single- and Dual-Colour In Vivo Ca2+ Imaging in Oligodendrocyte Precursor Cells and Neurons in Zebrafish.
abstract: In vivo time-lapse microscopy of genetically encoded biosensors allows for the optical interrogation of cell physiology. Here, we describe a protocol for single- and multi-channel imaging and analysis of Ca2+ signalling dynamics in oligodendrocyte precursor cells and surrounding neurones using cell type-specific expression of genetically encoded Ca2+ indicators. With this method, we can simultaneously investigate the spatiotemporal signalling activity in up to two cell types.

title: Analysis of Myelination and Oligodendrocytes in Zebrafish.
abstract: Zebrafish have emerged as a powerful model to study myelination and oligodendrocyte dynamics due to their optical transparency and regenerative capacity. This chapter provides a comprehensive set of protocols for analyzing oligodendrocytes and myelination in zebrafish embryos and larvae and also adults. We describe step-by-step methods for live imaging using transgenic lines, whole-mount and sectioned immunohistochemistry, and Western blot analysis. These approaches allow detailed spatial and temporal resolution of oligodendrocyte markers in vivo, ex vivo, and in vitro, facilitating the investigation of developmental myelination and remyelination following injury.

title: In Vitro Myelination Using DRG Explants: An Efficient Model for Quantitative Evaluation of Peripheral Nerve Myelination in Culture.
abstract: In vitro myelination, involving Schwann cells and dorsal root ganglion neurons, is an indispensable tool for studying the myelination process and evaluating the effects of various interventions under both physiological and pathological conditions in the peripheral nervous system. Here, we describe our DRG explant-based in vitro myelination (IVDME) culture method, which achieves more efficient myelination compared to conventional in vitro approaches.

title: Pathophysiology of Neuropathic Pain in Multiple Sclerosis: a Review.
abstract: Neuropathic pain is one of the most relevant symptoms in multiple sclerosis (MS) and is a key contributor to the impaired quality of life in this disease. A better understanding of MS-related neuropathic pain is needed to develop new drugs and improve the use of available ones. In this review, we cover existing knowledge on the pathophysiology of neuropathic pain in patients with MS. Our current understanding of this disorder stems from studies conducted on MS, other diseases responsible for neuropathic pain, and animal models of demyelinating disorders, like experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. Responsible mechanisms are complex and can act at different levels. At the molecular and cellular scale, neuronal hyperexcitability is the main driver of neuropathic pain; it is the final consequence of other interacting events taking place on the cell membrane and in the intracellular and extracellular environment. Impairment of inhibitory neurotransmission further enhances hyperexcitability. Functional alterations of complex neuronal networks can be observed at higher levels, showing that modifications of the dynamic pain connectome play a relevant role in the pathogenesis of pain. Moreover, in recent years a distinction has been drawn between neuropathic and nociplastic pain; the consequences of this new classification on pathophysiological models of MS-related neuropathic pain are not still fully understood and deserve future attention.

title: Roles of Folate-Dependent Epigenetic Modifications in Major Depressive Disorder.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a complex psychiatric condition that affects over 280 million individuals globally. MDD etiology remains undefined; however, recent research demonstrates a significant link between epigenetics and its underlying molecular mechanisms. Epigenetic modifications such as DNA and histone methylation require methyl groups, with S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) serving as the methyl-group donor generated through one-carbon metabolism. Folate plays a crucial role in regulating one-carbon metabolism, facilitating the conversion of methionine to SAM. MDD is increasingly associated with altered folate status, one-carbon metabolism, and epigenetic regulation in depression, although the extent to which these mechanisms contribute to MDD remains incompletely understood. This review consolidates evidence linking folate biology to epigenetic mechanisms in MDD, integrating findings from human observational and clinical studies with evidence from cellular and animal models. Overall, current evidence supports a biologically plausible connection between folate-dependent one-carbon metabolism and epigenetic regulation in MDD, while highlighting the need for further mechanistic and clinical studies to clarify these relationships and determine their potential therapeutic relevance.

title: Osteoporosis as a chronic disease: an expert narrative review and practical recommendations on long-term management and sequential therapy after denosumab discontinuation.
abstract: Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody that binds receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand, leading to marked and sustained reductions in fracture risk in osteoporosis. Due to its reversible mechanism and lack of skeletal retention, treatment interruption causes rebound bone turnover, accelerated bone mineral density (BMD) loss, and increased vertebral fracture risk. Optimising denosumab therapy therefore requires a long-term management strategy incorporating uninterrupted dosing and planned sequential antiresorptive therapy. This expert narrative review summarises evidence on denosumab pharmacology, efficacy, safety, and discontinuation management and provides practical recommendations informed by the published literature and the clinical experience of the author panel. No formal Delphi process, voting procedure, evidence-grading framework, or predefined consensus threshold was used. Main topics discussed included transition strategies after withdrawal, particularly alendronate (or zoledronic acid), timing of initiation, and biomarker-guided monitoring using serum C-terminal telopeptide (CTX). This paper also addresses management in special populations (chronic kidney disease, glucocorticoid exposure, malignancy, endocrine disorders) and evaluates health-system factors including infusion capacity, adherence, and coordinated primary-specialist care. Denosumab should not be discontinued without subsequent potent antiresorptive therapy. Sequential alendronate or zoledronic acid within six to seven months of the final injection, guided by CTX and BMD monitoring, is likely to be the most effective strategy in preventing rebound bone loss. Structured transition pathways are essential for sustained skeletal protection.

title: Therapeutic Potential of Formononetin in Drug-Resistant Epilepsy: Evidence from a Rotenone-PTZ-Lamotrigine Mouse Model.
abstract: Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) affects nearly one-third of individuals with epilepsy and remains a major therapeutic challenge despite the availability of multiple antiseizure medications. Mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic neuroinflammation, particularly NLRP3 inflammasome activation, are increasingly recognized as key contributors to pharmacoresistance. Formononetin, a plant-derived isoflavone, has shown anticonvulsant and neuroprotective effects in pentylenetetrazol (PTZ) kindled mice by restoring glutamate-GABA balance and attenuating neuroinflammatory signaling. The present study explored the therapeutic potential of formononetin in a rotenone-PTZ-lamotrigine mouse model of DRE. Mice were subjected to rotenone-adjuvant PTZ kindling in the presence of lamotrigine to induce a refractory seizure phenotype and were subsequently treated with formononetin. Seizure severity was quantified using the Racine scale, and GABA and glutamate levels were measured in whole-brain tissue. Oxidative and inflammasome-related changes were assessed by estimating NAD(P)H: quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO1), IL-1β, and caspase-1 in hippocampal and cortical regions using ELISA. We also evaluated astroglial and microglial activation by GFAP and Iba1 expression in the hippocampus and cortex. Formononetin treatment reduced seizure severity, improved the excitatory-inhibitory neurotransmitter balance, enhanced NQO1 levels, and attenuated IL-1β levels and caspase-1 activation, accompanied by a marked reduction in GFAP and Iba1-positive glial reactivity. These findings suggest that formononetin confers anticonvulsant and neuroprotective effects in a mitochondrial dysfunction-linked, lamotrigine-resistant epilepsy model, likely via coordinated modulation of oxidative defense, NLRP3-caspase-1 signaling, and glial activation. Formononetin thus emerges as a promising adjunctive candidate for managing drug-resistant epilepsy, warranting further mechanistic and translational investigation.

title: Intracerebral Administration of a Novel, Bioactive Peptide Induces a Biochemical Profile in Rat Brain Reminiscent of Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) presents a great unmet clinical need, but the much needed replication of the characteristic neuropathology in animal models has had limited success. Here, we provide in vivo evidence that T30, a bioactive peptide posited to drive AD, can induce in the rat brain a biochemical profile resembling AD pathology. Bilateral microinfusions of T30 into the medial septum/vertical diagonal band were administered twice a week for three weeks in rats. Although there was no effect on locomotor activity, novel object recognition and watermaze delayed-matching-to-place performance, T30 infusion reduced weight growth in the rats. Post mortem immunohistochemistry showed that T30 increased the AD biomarkers amyloid beta and phosphorylated tau in the cortex, hippocampus, and midbrain. Significant neuronal loss, indicated by reduced NeuN+ staining, was observed in brain tissue pooled from neocortex, hippocampus and midbrain. Further analysis showed a strong correlation between the 14mer T14, the active component of T30, and levels of its parent molecule acetylcholinesterase. However, this correlation only applied to protein levels, not enzymatic activity, suggesting independence from cholinergic transmission. Together, these findings support a non-cholinergic, peptide-driven mechanism by which T30 contributes to Alzheimer's-like neurodegeneration.

title: Myristoylated alanine rich C kinase substrate (MARCKS) and its role in the pathogenesis of cancer.
abstract: Myristoylated alanine-rich C kinase substrate (MARCKS) is primarily phosphorylated by protein kinase C (PKC). Recently, we have shown that it is also phosphorylated upon stimulation of ErbB2 (also known as HER2). It is localized to the plasma membrane and is an actin filament cross-linking protein. Phosphorylation or binding to calcium-calmodulin disrupts its association with the plasma membrane, leading to its translocation to the cytoplasm. The protein is involved in structural modulation of the actin cytoskeleton, chemotaxis, motility, cell adhesion, phagocytosis, and exocytosis through lipid sequestering and/or protein docking to membranes. It exerts an influence on many physiological processes, for example, embryonic development, tissue regeneration, neuronal plasticity, and inflammation. Increasingly, the role of MARCKS in the pathogenesis of cancers is being appreciated. The increased expression of either MARCKS or its phosphorylated form is associated with many cancers and is correlated with an adverse outcome. However, in some, it functions as a tumor suppressor gene, and decreased expression correlates with a favorable outcome. Despite these associations from in vitro experiments and some xenograft studies, the role of MARCKS in malignant transformation is poorly understood. Interestingly, specific peptide inhibitors derived from MARCKS inhibit its function and are being evaluated in cancers. This review is a critical assessment of the role of MARCKS in the pathogenesis of cancers, clarifies unanswered questions and suggests the way forward for the future.

title: Revealing Pharmacological Target for Comorbid Epilepsy in Alzheimer's Disease: Neurochemical Insights from STZ Mice.
abstract: Despite growing evidences of shared neurochemical alterations linked to comorbid epilepsy in AD, effective unified therapeutic strategies remain lacking. Thus, the present investigation was designed to identify shared neurochemical changes associated with lowered convulsive threshold in STZ (streptozotocin) model of AD-type dementia to pharmacologically address this comorbidity. Swiss albino mice were injected STZ (3 mg/kg, ICV) to induce AD-like pathology. On day 22nd, STZ mice were divided into two groups: one group served as AD control (STZ) and another group (STZ + PTZ) received PTZ (35 mg/kg) kindling to assess the reduced epileptogenesis threshold while naïve served as negative control. One more group was involved as epileptic control (PTZ). All groups underwent behavioral assessment using elevated plus maze, novel object recognition test and radial arm maze. Mice were euthanized on day 48th to collect the brain samples. The brain homogenate was used to assess redox status (GSH, TBARS and ROS), acetylcholinesterase (AChE) activity, amyloid and tau protein expression, histological alterations for specific disease pathology. As well as for neurochemical analysis to assess the shared neurochemical targets associated with comorbid epilepsy in AD. STZ mice were subjected to PTZ kindling exhibited significant greater seizure severity. The kindled status achieved by the sixth injection of PTZ, indicating reduced epileptogenic threshold. Behavioural results indicated significant cognitive impairment in STZ + PTZ treated mice compared with naive mice in EPM, NORT and RAM test. Significantly increased oxidative stress and cholinergic dysfunctions observed in STZ + PTZ mice. Neurochemical analysis revealed augmented excitatory neurotransmitter levels, along with declined glycine, GABA, taurine and arginine in STZ + PTZ mice. Moreover, reduced levels of monoamines and their metabolites reflect cognitive deficits in STZ and STZ + PTZ mice. This increased susceptibility to seizures was accompanied by significantly increased oxidative stress and excitatory neurotransmission in STZ + PTZ mice. Collectively, these observations suggest that AD related neurodegeneration may predispose to epileptogenesis further aggravate neurochemical changes. Our findings suggest that taurine, arginine and monoamines may serve as a shared neurochemical target for comorbid epilepsy in AD-type dementia.

title: Gray matter alterations and their atlas-based spatial associations with neurotransmitter distributions in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder.
abstract: Multiple neurotransmitter systems are implicated in the pathophysiology of isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) and its progression to α-synucleinopathy. This study aimed to identify baseline gray matter (GM) alterations in patients with iRBD compared with healthy controls and to examine their spatial correspondence with known neurotransmitter distributions. We further characterized GM patterns associated with future phenoconversion and their neurochemical context. A total of 109 patients with iRBD who completed at least one follow-up evaluation and 24 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural magnetic resonance imaging. Gray matter volume (GMV) alterations were assessed using the CAT12 toolbox. Spatial correlations between group-level GMV difference maps and neurotransmitter atlases were evaluated using the JuSpace toolbox. At baseline, patients with iRBD showed reduced GMV in the right cerebellar cortex and vermis, along with increased GMV in the left putamen and pallidum. These GMV alterations demonstrated significant spatial correspondence with dopaminergic receptor and transporter maps, including dopamine D2 receptors and the dopamine transporter (DAT). Among patients with iRBD, those who subsequently phenoconverted exhibited lower baseline GMV in the right medial orbital gyrus compared with non-converters. This pattern showed significant spatial correlations with serotonergic (5-HT2A), glutamatergic (mGluR5), GABAergic (GABAa), and dopaminergic (FDOPA) neurotransmitter maps. Patients with iRBD exhibit distinct patterns of GMV alteration that spatially align with dopaminergic neurotransmitter distribution maps, while phenoconversion is associated with GM changes corresponding to multiple neurotransmitter systems, although the phenoconversion findings are exploratory.

title: Managing trastuzumab deruxtecan-related adverse events in patients with metastatic breast cancer: insights from a worldwide survey of the Hermione EDUcational project.
journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has shown remarkable efficacy in phase III trials in patients with HER2-positive early- and late-stage breast cancer and HER2-low/ultra-low metastatic breast cancer (mBC). However, toxicities remain prevalent and clinically relevant, leading to dose reductions/interruptions or discontinuation. A survey was conducted across oncologists in 13 countries worldwide to collect experiences in managing T-DXd-related toxicities, focusing on nausea/vomiting, fatigue, and interstitial lung disease (ILD) as key areas of clinical concern. Ninety-nine experts participated in the survey. Nausea and fatigue were the most common toxicities, reported by 91.9% and 94.9% of respondents, respectively. 5-HT3 receptor antagonists, NK1 receptor antagonists, and corticosteroids were "very often" prescribed for prophylaxis. The frequency of use of second‑generation 5‑HT3 receptor antagonists varied among respondents. Most frequently, they employed an NK1 receptor antagonist combined with corticosteroids and 5‑HT3 receptor antagonists. Forty-four percent of respondents prescribed 4‑drug regimens incorporating NK1 receptor antagonists and olanzapine to all patients with nausea/vomiting above grade 1 in the first cycle, 35% reserved them for high‑risk patients, and 21% used them for all patients from cycle one. For all respondents, patients receiving T‑DXd experienced fatigue, with 65% observing it in more than 60% of patients, and most considered nausea/vomiting and fatigue to moderately or significantly affect daily activities and quality of life. ILD was reported as rare or occasional and was generally monitored using computed tomography. Real-life management of T-DXd-related toxicities is complex and needs an ongoing comprehensive evaluation of patients before, during and after therapy, with a highly trained/skilled multidisciplinary team.

title: Leveraging immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and neuropathology to identify the clinical value of different blood tau species in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Advances in plasma-based assays have allowed for the study of several tau and p-tau epitopes. P-tau217 has emerged as one of the most robust markers of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology. Despite their strong diagnostic performance, plasma tau biomarkers require further validation to clarify their clinical utility. To investigate the associations between a panel of phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated tau species measured in antemortem plasma and clinical features of autopsy-confirmed AD. Cross-sectional data from 123 participants from the BU ADRC who had antemortem blood draws and brain donation following death. Participants completed neuropsychological testing during life as part of their National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center-Uniform Data Set (NACC UDS) evaluation. AD neuropathology was diagnosed using NIA-Reagan criteria. Time interval between testing at last visit and autopsy ranged from 0 to 12 years, mean = 5.54 years. Raw neuropsychological test scores were used for analysis. Sample size ranged from 65 to 91 across the tests. Plasma samples were analyzed using immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry (IP-MS) for phosphorylated tau species (p-tau-181, 199, 202, 205, 217, 231) and non-phosphorylated tau (195-209, 212-221) peptides. Two ratios were analyzed, p-tau217/tau212-221 and p-tau205/tau195-209. 123 participants took part in this study, 55 (44.7%) female, and 6 (4.9%) Black/African American. The mean (SD) age at blood draw was 78.17 (8.55). The strongest association between plasma biomarkers with neuropsychological test outcomes was observed with the ratio p-tau217/tau212-221 (b = - 0.564-0.404, plow-high = 0.00-0.18), followed by p-tau217 (b = - 0.478-0.377, plow-high = 0.00-0.28), both significantly correlating with six of the eight neuropsychological measures (p < 0.05). Followed by the ratio p-tau205/tau195-209 (b = - 0.513-0.356, plow-high = 0.00-0.55), p-tau205 (b = - 0.365-0.226, plow-high = 0.00-0.44), then p-tau231 (b = - 0.319-0.237, plow-high = 0.02-0.62). Fewer significant relationships and weaker effect sizes were observed among the other biomarkers. The effect sizes of the ratio p-tau217/tau212-221, followed closely by p-tau217 on neuropsychological test outcomes, were observed to be the most similar to the effect sizes of autopsy-confirmed AD (b = - 0.564-0.393). Plasma p-tau217 and p-tau ratios were comparable to autopsy-confirmed AD in predicting clinical outcomes of AD. This study highlights the promise and potential utility of plasma biomarkers for symptom monitoring.

title: Countermanding saccades in children.
abstract: The countermanding saccade task is a widely used test of reactive inhibitory oculomotor control. The test comprises "Go" trials, in which saccades are directed towards target onsets, interspersed with "Stop" trials, where a signal sometime after target onset indicates that a saccade should be withheld or "countermanded". Computational models of the task assume a race to threshold between internal go and stop processes, the outcome of which determines whether a programmed response is cancelled. In this study, 181 typically developing primary-school-aged children completed child-friendly versions of the task. Three experiments examined the effect of task instruction (either to countermand saccades or ignore stop signals), stop signal characteristics (with and without an overlapping fixation cue) and practice (one versus two blocks). Children often failed to make saccades even when they were instructed to ignore the signal and make a response to the target on every trial. Saccade reaction times were longer on Stop compared with correct Go trials and significant "dips" (reductions in expected response frequency within discrete time bins) were observed in reaction time distributions associated with the change in the colour of the fixation stimulus that served as a stop signal. It is concluded that visual stop signals exert an exogenous inhibitory effect on saccades which decreases with increasing age. As such, care should be taken in interpreting the oculomotor stop signal task as a straightforward test of developing inhibitory control or the maturation of an internal stop process. OPEN ACCESS STATEMENT: Experiment task code, raw trial-level data, and analysis files for all experiments are available via the Open Science Framework: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/Q4PGH . The study protocol was not preregistered.

title: Protein Quality Control Systems in Neurodegeneration-Chaperones, Cytoskeleton, and the Pathogenic Transition of Tau.
abstract: Maintenance of protein homeostasis is essential for neuronal survival, and its disruption is a defining feature of neurodegenerative diseases. Neurons are particularly vulnerable to proteostatic stress due to their post-mitotic nature, long lifespan, and dependence on cytoskeletal integrity for structural stability, intracellular transport, and synaptic function. In tauopathies and related neurodegenerative disorders, misfolded proteins and aggregation-prone proteins burden the cellular quality-control systems, leading to cytoskeletal destabilization, synaptic dysfunction, and progressive neuronal loss. This review is organized around a central question: for a given tau species, defined by its isoform, post-translational modifications, and assembly state, what determines its fate? We examine how molecular chaperone networks, including HSP100, HSP90, HSP70, J-domain proteins (JDPs), small heat shock proteins (sHSPs), and the Prefoldin-CCT pathway, regulate the folding, disaggregation, sequestration, and degradation of pathogenic tau. We highlight how these chaperone networks influence key proteostasis checkpoints, determine whether tau refolds, is degraded, or is redirected toward toxic aggregation, and how these outcomes impact microtubule stability and neuronal function. Drawing on studies in yeast, Drosophila, mammalian models, and human tissues, we develop two key conclusions. First, chaperone activity is not uniformly protective against tauopathies; its effects depend on the tau species, cellular context, and disease stage. Second, because the cytoskeleton is both a chaperone client and an essential component of intracellular clearance pathways, tau pathology and proteostasis failure can reinforce one another. Finally, we discuss emerging therapeutic strategies and challenges in targeting chaperone networks to restore proteostasis while avoiding unintended neurotoxic consequences.

title: Subcutaneous apomorphine and the nonmotor features of Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a heterogeneous, progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which nonmotor manifestations (autonomic, sleep-related, neuropsychiatric, and sensory) constitute integral components of the disease continuum, exerting a disproportionate influence on quality of life, long-term disability, and caregiver burden. These features comprise both persistent components intrinsic to neurodegeneration and state-dependent fluctuations mechanistically linked to the oscillating dopaminergic tone imposed by pulsatile oral therapy. Apomorphine occupies a singular pharmacological position among the PD armamentarium, distinguished by a receptor binding profile, physicochemical properties, and pharmacokinetics that set it apart from other dopamine agonists and from levodopa-based therapies. Nearly four decades of clinical experience have established its efficacy in attenuating motor fluctuations and dyskinesias via continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSAI). Its effects on the nonmotor dimension of PD remain however incompletely characterized, reflecting both limited research investment and methodological constraints inherent to nonmotor outcome assessment and to apomorphine therapy itself. This narrative review and expert opinion examines the pharmacological basis for apomorphine's putative nonmotor efficacy, clinical evidence across individual nonmotor domains and iatrogenic considerations before reassessing apomorphine's therapeutic positioning within the device-aided therapy landscape. Nonmotor features should be regarded as primary determinants of treatment decision-making rather than secondary endpoints. The emerging concept of "fluctuation-dominant" PD provides a framework in which nonmotor fluctuation burden alone may constitute sufficient indication for CSAI, with direct implications for patient selection, timing of initiation, and redefinition of therapeutic goals beyond motor control.

title: Improving Descriptive Diagnostics of Autism in People With Moderate or Severe Intellectual Disabilities: A Qualitative Participatory Study.
journal: Journal of autism and developmental disorders
abstract: This study aimed to improve descriptive autism assessment for people with moderate to severe intellectual disabilities (ID) in the Netherlands. The goal was to co-design a framework including an overview of assessment instruments, and recommendations for evaluating broader functioning, for translating findings into daily care and for involving representatives and staff. We used a participatory design, involving parents/representatives, clinicians, care staff, and management from ID and mental health services. The process included a literature study of autism-related instruments, a Delphi study to reach consensus on suitable instruments, and four focus group discussions (FGDs) exploring stakeholder involvement and the role of assessment instruments in the diagnostic process. The literature study identified 20 relevant instruments, of which 13 were selected through the Delphi study (n=37, three rounds). Key selection criteria included low burden for individuals, use of multiple information sources, and strong psychometric quality. While quick assessments were preferred, concerns arose about oversimplifying the autism assessment. FGDs (n=5-12) highlighted eight themes on stakeholder involvement, focusing on timing, roles, and goals. Although no consensus emerged on an optimal combination of tools, clarity about an instrument's purpose and implications proved important. The final FGD identified five potentially overlapping phases in the diagnostic process. The co-designed framework provides an overview of instruments for the assessment of autism and emphasises early and continuous involvement of parents and caregivers. Their participation is essential for defining concerns, guiding assessment goals, sharing information, and applying diagnostic outcomes to improve daily care and support.

title: Visual external focus of attention modulates corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance after acute exercise.
abstract: Individuals are frequently instructed to adopt an internal focus during exercise, such as concentrating on a specific muscle, which may inadvertently lead to online conscious motor processing and constrain automatic motor control. In contrast, an external focus, particularly with distant visual feedback, is thought to benefit corticospinal modulation, enhancing automaticity and movement complexity. Nonetheless, the effective integration of attentional focus into evidence-based exercise prescription requires a mechanistic understanding of its neurophysiological basis. Therefore, this study investigated whether a single exercise bout performed with visual external, external or internal focus differentially modulates corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance (Corticospinal Excitability/Silent Period ratio), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), intracortical facilitation (ICF) and torque complexity. Thirty-seven healthy young adults were randomised to internal (12), external (12), or visual external focus (13) groups, completing a seated calf-raise bout to failure under the respective focus of attention instruction. Neurophysiological outcomes were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and analysed in a linear mixed-effects model. Corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance was enhanced after an exercise bout carried out with a visual external focus (increase 1.40 ± 0.42 mV/s, p = 0.005), while no changes were detected with an external or internal focus (all p ≥ 0.05). SICI, ICF and torque complexity showed no significant effect regarding attentional focus. The present study contributes to the neurophysiological basis for using goal-oriented visual feedback cues to increase corticospinal drive, offering a targeted intervention strategy which has potential to optimize motor performance in elite athletes and accelerate functional recovery in clinical populations. The present study was registered under NCT06538766 on 26/07/2024.

title: Longitudinal plasma protein profiling in glioblastoma patients using NULISAseq reveals treatment-associated changes across radiation and chemotherapy.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor with poor outcomes despite surgery, radiotherapy (RT), and temozolomide (TMZ). Monitoring relies on imaging, which is confounded by pseudoprogression and provides limited molecular insight. Circulating biomarkers may offer a minimally invasive approach to track disease and treatment effects. We performed targeted longitudinal proteomic profiling of plasma from post-surgery GBM patients (n = 11) at baseline (pre-radiotherapy (RT)), after RT with concomitant TMZ, and after adjuvant TMZ, alongside healthy controls (n = 15), using the NULISAseq CNS panel covering 131 proteins related to neurodegeneration, neuroinflammation, and vascular health. Differential expressions were assessed using volcano plots, hierarchical clustering, paired statistical comparisons and longitudinal trends analysis. At baseline, GBM plasma showed elevated markers of neuroaxonal and glial injury, extracellular matrix regulators, and inflammatory signaling compared to controls. Several established neurodegeneration and Alzheimer's disease- related biomarkers were also higher in GBM plasma versus controls. Following radiotherapy and concomitant TMZ, cytokines including IL10, IL5, and IL33 increased, indicating systemic immune activation, while BDNF showed a modest decline. Adjuvant TMZ treatment attenuated radiotherapy-induced cytokine elevations and reduced neuronal injury markers, suggesting therapy-driven reduction of inflammatory and neurodegenerative signals. Longitudinal analysis confirmed dynamic shifts in specific proteins across baseline, radiotherapy, and TMZ phases. High-sensitivity plasma proteomics suggested therapy-induced changes in CNS-specific and immune markers in GBM, highlighting candidate biomarkers that can be further developed for real-time monitoring of treatment response. These findings suggest candidate circulating markers that may complement imaging for monitoring disease biology and therapeutic response, and warrant validation in larger cohorts.

title: Adolescents During the Pandemic: Supportive and In-Person Rather Than Digital Social Connections Are Associated With Lower Sadness.
journal: The Journal of adolescent health : official publication of the Society for Adolescent Medicine
abstract: Social connections support emotional well-being and act as buffer against depression during challenging life episodes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, adolescent's social connectedness was disrupted. Here, we examined the association between social connectedness and sadness in a large US sample of adolescents during the pandemic. As part of the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development Study, adolescents completed two online surveys around May (n = 5,298, mage: 12.5 years, 49.7% female) and August 2020 (n = 5,051, mage: 12.7, 49.0% female), including the National Institute of Health Toolbox Sadness Questionnaire short form, and questions about relationship quality, parent-child engagement, and digital connections. Mixed linear models tested associations between social connection and sadness with time points as covariate, sadness was compared between clusters sharing social characteristics. In independent models, household conflicts were associated with higher sadness (p < .01), whereas positive parent-child engagement and relationships, such as having dinner together and talking with parents about plans, were associated with lower sadness (p < .01). Texting, social media, and video chat time were associated with greater sadness (p < .01). Clusters with lower digital communications, stronger parent-child engagement, and better relationships, showed the lowest sadness score. Shifting to less digital connections from May to August was associated with a stronger sadness decrease (p < .01). In-person, rather than digital, and nonconflictual social connections were associated with lower sadness in adolescents in the pandemic context, emphasizing differences between proximal and remote social connections, and possible emotional costs of over-reliance on remote, digital forms of interaction.

title: Stability of Acyclovir, Aprepitant, Glibenclamide, and Mebendazole Oral Suspensions Compounded with SyrSpend® SF PH4.
abstract: Pharmaceutical compounding provides individualized oral dosage forms for patients who cannot use commercially available medicines; however, formulation-specific stability data are required to establish appropriate beyond-use dates (BUDs). This study evaluated the physical, chemical, and microbiological stability of oral suspensions containing acyclovir 40 mg/mL (200 mg/5 mL), aprepitant 20 mg/mL, glibenclamide (glyburide) 0.2 mg/mL, or mebendazole 10 mg/mL compounded with SyrSpend® SF PH4. The formulations were stored at room temperature (15-30 °C) and under refrigeration (2-8 °C) and evaluated at 0, 7, 14, 30, 60, and 90 days. Chemical stability was assessed in six replicates at each time point using validated high-performance liquid chromatography methods, with an acceptance criterion of 90.0%-110.0% of the nominal concentration. Physical appearance, pH, and microbiological quality were also monitored throughout the study. No changes in color, odor, phase separation, precipitation, or apparent viscosity were observed during the supported stability periods, and pH values did not deviate from their initial values by more than 0.5 pH unit. Acyclovir 40 mg/mL (200 mg/5 mL), aprepitant 20 mg/mL, and mebendazole 10 mg/mL remained physically, chemically, and microbiologically stable for 90 days under both storage conditions. Glibenclamide (glyburide) 0.2 mg/mL supported a BUD of 90 days at room temperature and 60 days under refrigeration. These findings provide scientifically supported BUDs for four compounded oral suspensions. Under the conditions studied, SyrSpend® SF PH4 was a suitable vehicle for preparing these individualized oral formulations when appropriate commercially available dosage forms are unavailable.

title: Stability Testing of Intraventricular Irrigations Diluted in Lactated Ringer's Solution.
abstract: To evaluate the physical and chemical stability of minute concentrations of daptomycin, nicardipine, tobramycin, and vancomycin diluted in lactated ringer's solution (LR) in concentrations safe for administration via IRRAflow intrathecal irrigation. Commercially available vials of daptomycin, nicardipine, tobramycin and vancomycin were used to compound intraventricular irrigations in LR. The LR irrigations that were tested include daptomycin 2mg/1000mL, nicardipine 2.5mg/1000mL, tobramycin 4mg/1000mL and vancomycin 4mg/1000mL. All irrigations were stored at room temperature and were not protected from light. Samples for each irrigation were tested at various timepoints via Ultra-High Performance Liquid Chromatography-Tandem Mass Spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS) testing in conjunction with visual inspection, pH testing, and light absorbance plating to determine if precipitation occurred. Samples were considered chemically stable if they retained 90% of their initial concentration. All samples were found to be chemically and physically stable within the tested timepoints except for nicardipine. Vancomycin, daptomycin, and tobramycin were found to be chemically and physically stable at 12 hours. Nicardipine had more than 10% degradation at eight hours yet maintained stability at four hours after compounding. By extrapolating the degradation of nicardipine, our results demonstrate that the compound maintained a concentration greater than 90% at six hours. With the use of UHPLC-MS/MS, pH testing, and calorimetric absorbance measurement, we found that daptomycin, tobramycin and vancomycin were physically and chemically stable in LR out to 12 hours at room temperature. Nicardipine was found to maintain stability out to 6 hours at room temperature.

title: Long-Term Stability of a Fixed-Dose Doxazosin and Finasteride Combination Formulation.
abstract: Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) are commonly treated with a1-adrenoreceptor antagonists, 5a-reductase inhibitors, or a combination of both. The development of a fixed-dose doxazosin (DOX) and finasteride (FIN) formulation in a single dosage form is expected to improve efficacy, lower cost, and improve adherence to the treatment of male LUTS/BPH. The study aims to determine the stability of a fixed-dose combination formulation containing doxazosin (1 mg) and finasteride (5 mg). We conducted long-term stability studies of a fixed-dose DOX-FIN combination capsule. A stability-indicating HPLC method was developed and used to determine DOX and FIN in combination capsules simultaneously. DOX-FIN capsules were stored at 4°C, 25°C, and 40°C for 12 months. Samples were analyzed periodically using the HPLC method. The HPLC analysis showed that both DOX and FIN amounts remained above 90% of the initial values after 1 year when the capsules were stored at 4°C and 25°C. An elevated temperature (40°C) is not a recommended storage condition for the compounded capsules. Even at 40 °C, doxazosin stability remains above 90% up to 30 days, and finasteride remains above 90% up to 90 days. Long-term stability studies indicated that the combination of doxazosin and finasteride remained stable, with 90% of the drug still present in the formulation after one year for capsules stored at 4°C and 25°C.

title: Topical Ketoprofen 5%, Amitriptyline HCL 5%, and Lidocaine 5% Compounded in VersaPro Cream for Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: A Case Report.
abstract: Peripheral neuropathy is a common complication of type 1 and type 2 diabetes, often resulting in severe pain that significantly impacts the quality of life. This case report describes the treatment of a 56-year-old female patient with severe peripheral neuropathic pain in the lower extremities due to type 1 diabetes after pain persisted while using conventional therapy. The patient was prescribed a compounded topical cream containing Ketoprofen 5%, Amitriptyline HCL 5%, and Lidocaine 5% in VersaPro Cream Base to help address symptoms of diabetic peripheral neuropathy in addition to her systemic medications. Over an 8-week treatment period, the patient reported significant reductions in pain intensity and improved functional outcomes, including sleep quality and mobility. This case highlights the potential benefit of compounded topical analgesics as an adjunct therapy for managing neuropathic pain in patients with limited treatment options, and when conventional options may not be suitable.

title: Semi-Automated Integration of Motor Healthspan and Lifespan Analysis Using FlyTrDT Pipeline in Drosophila melanogaster.
abstract: Aging is characterized by progressive functional decline and reduced lifespan; these two parameters are often evaluated independently in experimental studies. In Drosophila melanogaster, lifespan assays and negative geotaxis-based locomotor measurements are commonly used to study aging and neurodegeneration. However, there is a lack of standardized frameworks that quantitatively integrate early motor performance with long-term survival. Here, we describe a reproducible, semi-automated workflow that combines lifespan analysis with objective quantification of motor healthspan in aging flies. The protocol integrates controlled fly rearing conditions, mortality accounting, and video-based negative geotaxis assays using standardized MP4 recordings (minimum 1280 × 720 resolution, 30 frames/s). Locomotor performance is quantified using a custom Python-based pipeline implemented in Python 3.12.1 with OpenCV 4.9.0, NumPy 1.26.4, Pandas 2.2.0, and Matplotlib 3.5.2. The workflow performs frame-by-frame centroid detection and extracts active climbing slope (pixels/s) as a continuous metric of motor function. Survival trajectories are analyzed by calculating the survival fraction and performing trapezoidal numerical integration to obtain the survival area under the curve (AUC). Normalization of early motor performance enables direct comparison between functional decline and overall longevity. The workflow was evaluated by comparing semi-automated climbing slope measurements with conventional manual endpoint scoring in control and amyloid-β-expressing flies, with both methods detecting age-dependent motor decline. Representative datasets demonstrated reproducible lifespan trajectories in Canton S controls and measurable early motor impairment in the neurodegenerative model. This method minimizes observer bias, enhances reproducibility, and remains compatible with low-cost video acquisition systems. The workflow can be readily adapted to genetic models, pharmacological interventions, and neurodegenerative paradigms, providing a scalable platform for integrated aging phenotyping in Drosophila.

title: Adjunctive Trazodone Effects on Sleep, Mood, and Circulating 5-HT and BDNF in Depression.
abstract: This retrospective study evaluated the association of adjunctive trazodone with sleep architecture, sleep quality, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and circulating 5-HT and BDNF levels in patients with depression. A total of 156 propensity-score-matched patients were included in the final analysis, including 78 who received conventional antidepressant therapy (fluvoxamine monotherapy; control group) and 78 who received combined trazodone and fluvoxamine therapy (observation group). Both treatment regimens were continued for 8 consecutive weeks. Propensity score matching (PSM) was used to balance baseline characteristics between the groups. Sleep architecture, sleep quality, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and circulating 5-HT and BDNF levels were assessed at the prespecified clinical time points. Compared with the control group, the observation group demonstrated significantly reduced awake time, prolonged rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and slow-wave sleep (SWS) duration, improved sleep quality, and lower depression and anxiety scores at week 4 (HAMD: 8.23 ± 1.25 vs. 11.88 ± 2.50; HAMA: 4.35 ± 1.32 vs. 7.89 ± 2.17; both P < 0.001), together with higher circulating 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels at week 8. Furthermore, the overall clinical response rate was significantly higher in the observation group than in the control group. These findings suggest that adjunctive trazodone was associated with better sleep-related and clinical outcomes, as well as higher circulating 5-HT and BDNF levels, than fluvoxamine monotherapy.

title: A Pilot Retrospective Electronic Health Record Workflow for Evaluating Adjunctive Danshen Injection After Acute Myocardial Infarction.
abstract: Danshen injection is used as an adjunctive cardiovascular therapy in some Chinese hospitals, but retrospective evaluations are vulnerable to exposure misclassification, nonuniform measurement timing, baseline imbalance, complete-case selection, and time-related bias. This article presents an audit-ready electronic health record workflow for adults with acute myocardial infarction who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention and received inpatient aspirin plus clopidogrel. The workflow adds TCM-specific fields for syndrome differentiation, indication, prescriber specialty, product formulation, and administration timing; separates outcome-specific analysis sets; and defines propensity-score overlap weighting for the population with clinical equipoise. An archived 89-patient cohort (45 with documented Danshen administration and 44 controls) illustrates the analytical sequence. In the archived file, only analysis-file checks, model fitting, balance diagnostics, bootstrap estimation, and visualization could be executed. Source-record steps requiring unrecovered treatment timestamps, echocardiographic metadata, assay boundaries, exact exclusion variables, or adjudicated events are presented as workflow specifications and were not treated as completed procedures. The groups were strongly imbalanced at baseline. In the primary ANCOVA using HC3 standard errors, the adjusted between-group difference in pre-discharge left ventricular ejection fraction was 6.82 percentage points (95% confidence interval, 4.54-9.10). The separate overlap-weighted estimate was 6.95 percentage points (patient-level bootstrap standard error: 1.08; 95% percentile confidence interval: 4.90-9.07; 2,000 resamples). These estimates are numerical demonstrations rather than causal treatment effects. Database-coded cardiovascular and bleeding indicators were excluded because component events, dates, follow-up completeness, and a common time origin could not be verified. The workflow has not been externally validated and should be considered a pilot demonstration.

title: Combination Therapy of Montelukast and Desloratadine in Pediatric Allergic Rhinitis: Effects on Symptoms and Inflammatory Markers.
abstract: This retrospective, controlled study evaluated the clinical outcomes of montelukast sodium combined with desloratadine syrup in pediatric patients with allergic rhinitis. Medical records from 360 children aged 6-12 years treated between October 2021 and November 2024 were reviewed. Patients were classified according to documented treatment as desloratadine monotherapy (Group A, n = 180) or desloratadine plus montelukast (Group B, n = 180). During the 4-week treatment period, Total Nasal Symptom Score (TNSS), Total Non-Nasal Symptom Score (TNNSS), time to symptom improvement, serum immunoglobulin E (IgE), interleukin-13 (IL-13), eosinophil counts, and adverse events were assessed. Group B had lower post-treatment TNSS (4.65 ± 2.12 vs 5.32 ± 2.09, p = 0.003) and TNNSS (1.96 ± 1.43 vs 2.48 ± 1.01, p < 0.001), and rhinorrhea improved sooner (10.38 ± 1.87 vs 13.48 ± 1.20 days, p < 0.001). Greater reductions were also observed in inflammatory markers, including IgE and IL-13 (90.36 ± 22.58 vs 102.78 ± 19.25 ng/L, p < 0.001). Adverse-event rates did not differ significantly (0.56% vs 1.67%; Fisher's exact test, p = 0.623), although only four events were recorded. These findings indicate that combination therapy was associated with greater improvements in clinical symptoms and inflammatory markers than desloratadine monotherapy; however, the retrospective, nonrandomized design and limited safety events require cautious interpretation.

title: Clinical approach to balance intensity in people with multiple sclerosis: clinical judgment versus the Balance Intensity Tool for Exercise - an inter-rater agreement and reliability study.
abstract: Balance training is essential for enhancing stability in people with multiple sclerosis (PwMS). However, guidance on exercise intensity remains vague and largely relies on clinical judgment as standardized assessment methods are absent. This study introduces and evaluates the Balance Intensity Tool for Exercise (BITE), a standardized method for assessment of balance intensity based on observable errors, and compares it with traditional clinical judgment. Sixty-one PwMS, recruited from physiotherapy clinics and social networks, performed two balance tasks: line-walking and tandem-stance. The tasks were videorecorded for subsequent intensity assessment. Intensity was rated using (1) BITE, where three assessors measured the percentage of time with observable errors as a measure of intensity, and (2) clinical judgment, where three experienced physiotherapists scored intensity on a 0-100 scale. Balance capacity was measured with the Mini-BESTest. BITE assessors and clinicians were blinded to each other's ratings. Inter-rater agreement, reliability, and measurement error were evaluated using Bland-Altman analysis with 95% Limits of Agreement (LoA), Intra-class Correlation Coefficient (ICC2,1), and Standard Error of Measurement (SEM). Associations with balance capacity were examined using Spearman's rank correlation. Intensities measured by BITE were consistently lower than clinical judgment (line-walking median: 36% vs. 74%; tandem-stance median: 23% vs. 53%). BITE demonstrated excellent inter‑rater reliability (ICC2,1 > 0.9). Narrower pairwise LoA (up to ±20% vs. up to ±36%) and lower SEM (up to 8.3 vs. up to 11.2) were observed when compared to clinical judgment. Both methods demonstrated identical correlations with balance performance as measured by the Mini-BESTest (Spearman's rho: -0.82). BITE provides a quantifiable method to describe balance exercise intensity in PwMS based on the time of observed performance errors. BITE demonstrated excellent inter-rater reliability and inter-rater agreement, with LoA ≤ 20%, while clinical judgment exhibited wider LoA. Further research should explore its applicability in other populations with impaired balance.

title: A Protocol for Dissection, Immunostaining and Mounting of the Drosophila Visual System.
abstract: The Drosophila visual system is a powerful model for exploring how neuronal diversity is generated and integrated into functional neural circuits - a central question in developmental neuroscience. It comprises the retina and four distinct neuropils: the lamina, medulla, lobula, and lobula plate, which together form a highly organized structure that processes visual input from the retina and relays it to the higher centers of the brain. During development, the visual system undergoes significant remodeling. During larval development, neuroblasts are progressively generated from the neuroepithelium and divide asymmetrically to produce diverse neuronal subtypes by integrating spatial and temporal patterning programs. These neurons then differentiate and form precise synaptic connections that build the functional circuits of the adult visual system. These dynamic processes can be reliably studied using immunostaining across larval, pupal, and adult stages. Herein, we provide a detailed, reproducible protocol for dissecting and immunostaining the developing and adult Drosophila visual system. We primarily focus on representative imaging of larval neuroblasts to highlight spatiotemporal patterning and neuronal specification, and to visualize adult neuropil morphology. This provides a robust framework for visualizing the developing Drosophila visual system.

title: Neuroinflammation-Associated Synaptic Dysfunction in Neurodegenerative Diseases: A Dual-Database Parallel Bibliometric Analysis.
abstract: Neuroinflammation-associated synaptic dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a convergent pathological process across neurodegenerative diseases; however, the development, knowledge structure, and emerging directions of this interdisciplinary field remain incompletely characterized. Here, we present a structured bibliometric workflow for retrieving, curating, and analyzing bibliographic records from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus using a dual-database parallel design. Publications from 2000-2025 were independently retrieved, filtered, and processed, yielding 1,841 records from Web of Science and 2,429 records from Scopus. Bibliometrix, VOSviewer, CiteSpace, BiblioVista, and Scimago Graphica were used to characterize publication trends, disciplinary distributions, international collaboration, author and institutional networks, core journals and references, keyword co-occurrence, citation bursts, and thematic evolution. Both databases showed sustained growth in research output, with higher publication activity observed after 2015. The United States and China were among the leading contributors and highly connected participants in international collaboration networks. The intellectual and conceptual structures of the field were frequently characterized by recurring themes involving neuroinflammation, microglia, synaptic dysfunction, complement-mediated synaptic pruning, oxidative stress, synaptic plasticity, and neurodegenerative disease pathology. Temporal analyses showed evolving patterns in research themes, with increasing representation of studies related to neuroimmune synapse interactions and synaptic vulnerability. By retaining the two databases as independent analytical corpora rather than directly merging their records, this workflow enables descriptive comparison of shared and database-specific bibliometric patterns. The workflow provides a structured framework for mapping neuroinflammation-synapse research and may be adapted to other interdisciplinary biomedical fields.

title: Quantification of peri-ictal magnetic resonance imaging abnormalities (PMA) in status epilepticus: Clinical and prognostic significance of PMA volume.
abstract: Peri-ictal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormalities (PMA) are increasingly recognized in patients with status epilepticus (SE), but the clinical factors influencing their occurrence and extent remain incompletely understood. We aimed to quantify PMA and investigate the associations of PMA occurrence and volume with SE duration, etiology, and mortality. In this multicenter cohort study, comprising a retrospectively identified cohort and a prospectively recruited cohort, adult patients with SE who underwent brain MRI within 48 h of SE onset were included. PMA were identified on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and quantified using an automated postprocessing pipeline to calculate total PMA volume. Multivariable regression analyses were used to examine factors associated with PMA occurrence, extent, and mortality. Of 260 patients, 91 (35%) had PMA on DWI. In multivariable analyses, SE duration and etiology were independently associated with PMA occurrence and volume. SE lasting >60 min had higher odds of PMA (odds ratio [OR] = 3.90, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.79-8.82, p < .001) and significantly greater PMA volume, whereas acute triggering factors in patients with epilepsy were linked with lower odds (OR = .15, 95% CI = .05-.44, p < .001). PMA occurrence was associated with more than threefold higher odds of mortality (adjusted OR = 3.85, 95% CI = 1.55-10.24, p = .005). Each 10-fold increase in PMA volume was associated with 43% higher odds of mortality (adjusted OR = 1.43, 95% CI = 1.14-1.80, p = .002). In a sensitivity analysis restricted to in-hospital mortality, each 10-fold increase in PMA volume was associated with 47% higher odds of mortality (adjusted OR = 1.47, 95% CI = 1.15-1.89, p = .002). PMA extent is determined by SE duration and underlying etiology. Although MRI timing relative to SE termination could not always be determined, quantitative PMA assessment provides prognostic information beyond PMA presence alone, as increasing PMA volume is associated with progressively higher mortality. These findings support quantitative PMA burden as a potential imaging biomarker of SE severity and adverse outcome.

title: Brain PDGFRβ+ Cells Exhibit Diverse Reactive Phenotypes After Stroke Without Requiring KLF4.
abstract: The pathobiology of ischemic stroke is associated with the activation of brain platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR)β+ perivascular cells. While Krüppel-like factor (KLF)4 is a well-established mediator of peripheral PDGFRβ+ cell activation, its role in brain PDGFRβ+ cells remains elusive. Herein, we aimed to characterize the spatiotemporal reactivity of brain PDGFRβ+ cells, while assessing KLF4 contribution upon experimental ischemic stroke using transgenic mice that enable tracking PDGFRβ+ cells or conditionally depleting KLF4 in PDGFRβ+ cells. Moving beyond the qualitative descriptors, we sought to develop point pattern analysis (PPA) and topological data analysis (TDA) workflows to generate robust and reusable mathematical models to assess spatial cell responses and tissue scar topological changes. First, we report the emergence of phenotypically distinct reactive parenchymal PDGFRβ+ cells, which cannot be causally and exclusively linked, as it is currently proposed, to local cell proliferation or adjacent vascular detachment. Furthermore, we show that KLF4 is barely expressed in brain PDGFRβ+ cells under normal conditions and that it is only marginally induced in reactive PDGFRβ+ cells at the injured brain. Notably, the conditional attenuation of KLF4 expression specifically in reactive PDGFRβ+ cells does not alter spatial cellular distribution nor scar organization. This suggests that, in contrast to peripheral PDGFRβ+ cells upon ischemic insults, KLF4 is not a main regulator of the reactivity of brain cells in response to ischemic stroke. Ultimately, our findings supported by open-source spatiotemporal models indicate that the reactivity of brain PDGFRβ+ perivascular cells is highly heterogeneous and fundamentally distinct from peripheral PDGFRβ+ cells.

title: Amygdala Oligodendrocyte MDH1 Dysregulation and Mitochondrial Dysfunction in High Urea-Induced Anxiety-Like Behavior.
abstract: The high incidence and mortality rates of anxiety disorders in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have drawn attention. Prior studies identified urea as an independent risk factor for mental disorders in CKD. While urea accumulation is known to impair synaptic plasticity, its effects on glial cells remain unclear. How urea influences oligodendrocyte lineage differentiation may represent a critical node in neuron-glia interactions. Previous studies have shown that OL-lineage cells may be underrepresented in scRNA-seq datasets. We selected amygdala tissue from wild-type and high-urea (UT-B-/-) mice and performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), behavioral tests, and cellular experiments to delineate the impact of urea on oligodendrocyte lineage dynamics. In UT-B-/- mice, the relative abundance of oligodendrocyte subpopulations enriched for mitochondrial transcripts decreased, suggesting vulnerability to urea toxicity. Dlat and MDH1, genes associated with TCA cycle-related metabolism, were downregulated alongside alterations in mitochondrial and oxidative phosphorylation-related transcriptional programs. Urea dose-dependently decreased MDH1 expression, mitochondrial membrane potential, and intracellular ATP content in MO3.13 cells. Regulatory analyses linked MDH1 to energy metabolism and neurodegenerative pathways. Trajectory reconstruction suggested altered differentiation- and myelination-related transcriptional programs in mitochondria-related oligodendrocytes (MitOLs). The cytoplasmic concentration and fate of oxaloacetic acid (OAA) are regulated by the reversible catalysis of MDH1. OAA supplementation partially restored amygdalar MDH1 expression and alleviated anxiety-like behaviors in UT-B-/- mice, while improving mitochondrial bioenergetics in urea-exposed MO3.13 cells. These findings support a candidate metabolic-glial model linking elevated urea, MDH1 dysregulation, oligodendrocyte bioenergetic dysfunction, and anxiety-like behavior, with potential relevance to CKD-associated anxiety.

title: The balance of persistent inward and outward currents shapes bistable motoneuron firing: Digging deeper into ∆I and ∆F.
Synthetic Cells With Chemo-Optical Signaling Enable Targeted Capture and Killing of Bacteria.
abstract: Synthetic cells are molecularly defined systems which recreate life-like behaviors, yet their capacity to engage and act on living cells remains limited. Here, we engineer synthetic cells that combine optical and chemical signaling to achieve programmable capture and killing of bacteria with high spatial precision. To enable bacteria capture, giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) were functionalized with the blue light responsive protein BcLOV4, allowing light activatable adhesion to bacterial membranes. Encapsulation of Nanoluciferase allows the synthetic cells to generate an internal bioluminescent light signal, which activates BcLOV4 mediated bacterial recruitment without external illumination. For subsequent bacterial elimination, galactose oxidase was used to generate hydrogen peroxide locally at the GUV membranes, resulting in the selective killing of captured bacteria. This two-step mechanism mimics a key aspect of innate immune cells, namely localized pathogen elimination, and provides a blueprint for spatially precise antimicrobial synthetic cells.

title: Association Between Dietary Vitamin Intake and Short Sleep Duration Among Adults in the United States: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) Data.
abstract: Objective Short sleep duration (SSD) and inadequate dietary vitamin intake are both relevant to overall health and may share relationships with chronic disease risk. However, the relationship between dietary vitamin intake and sleep duration remains incompletely characterized, particularly when vitamin intake is evaluated relative to total energy consumption; additionally, limited research has been done to evaluate the relationship between SSD and vitamins that are not traditionally associated with sleep. Understanding these associations may help clarify potential nutritional factors related to sleep duration. This study evaluated associations between SSD and dietary intake of vitamins A, B1, B2, B3, B6, B9, B12, C, D, E, and K per 1,000 kilocalories among adults in the United States. Materials and methods This cross-sectional study used 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data. Adults aged ≥20 years with complete sleep, dietary, covariate, and Day 1 dietary weight data were included (n=4,169). SSD was defined as fewer than 7 hours of usual weekday/workday sleep. Primary endpoints were vitamins A, B6, and K; all other vitamins were secondary endpoints. Participants were categorized into low, middle, and high intake tertiles for each vitamin. Separate weighted logistic regression models were performed using the NHANES Day 1 dietary sample weight and adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, income-to-poverty ratio, total energy intake, and body mass index. NHANES strata and primary sampling units were not incorporated into the analysis. Results SSD prevalence decreased across low-to-high intake groups for vitamin A (24.2% to 16.4%), vitamin B6 (22.7% to 18.7%), and vitamin K (23.5% to 17.8%). Higher intake remained associated with lower odds of SSD for vitamin A (aOR=0.710, 95% CI 0.710-0.711), vitamin B6 (aOR=0.724, 95% CI 0.723-0.725), and vitamin K (aOR=0.815, 95% CI 0.814-0.816). Weaker inverse associations were observed for vitamins B1, B2, B3, B12, D, and E. Vitamin C demonstrated a nonlinear inverse pattern, whereas vitamin B9 showed a direct association. Conclusion Higher dietary intake of vitamins A, B6, and K was associated with lower odds of SSD among adults in the United States. Causation cannot be inferred because of the cross-sectional study design. In addition, confidence intervals and significance estimates should be interpreted cautiously because NHANES strata and primary sampling units were not incorporated into the analysis. Prospective studies using full complex survey methods are warranted to further evaluate these associations.

title: Electroconvulsive therapy for trunk and visceral cenesthopathy associated with major depressive disorder: A case series of three elderly women.
journal: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences
abstract: Severe cenesthopathy associated with major depressive disorder (MDD) may cause malnutrition and functional decline. We report three elderly women with trunk and visceral cenesthopathy associated with MDD who improved markedly following electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Case A: A woman in her 60s developed MDD while caring for her mother with dementia. Despite pharmacological treatment, trunk, limb, and oral cenesthopathy developed 6 months later, resulting in reduced food intake and physical deterioration. Symptoms improved after six ECT sessions, nearly resolved after 12, and ECT was completed after 15 sessions without recurrence. Case B: A woman in her 70s developed MDD after prolonged caregiving stress. Despite pharmacological treatment, she developed trunk and visceral cenesthopathy with organ displacement sensations, dyspnea, speech disturbance, and loss of appetite. Cenesthopathy resolved after three ECT sessions; dyspnea and speech disturbance improved after 10. ECT was completed after 13 sessions. After recurrence, a second acute ECT course followed by maintenance ECT maintained clinical stability. Case C: A woman in her 70s with longstanding MDD developed visceral and oral cenesthopathy after discontinuing antidepressants. Despite pharmacological treatment, she became unable to eat or drink. Cenesthopathy resolved after four ECT sessions, restoring oral intake. ECT was completed after eight sessions without recurrence. ECT may be an effective treatment for trunk and visceral cenesthopathy associated with MDD. Early consideration of ECT may be warranted when malnutrition or physical deterioration necessitates rapid symptom control.

title: The dual future of OPM-MEG: Clinical translation and naturalistic neuroscience.
abstract: Optically pumped magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) has moved beyond proof of principle. The decisive question is no longer whether cryogen-free sensors can detect neuromagnetic fields from the human brain with sufficient sensitivity, but whether complete systems can deliver clinical decision value and interpretable recordings during more naturalistic behaviour. Here we argue that OPM-MEG is developing along two partly overlapping trajectories. One is clinical translation, where usefulness depends more on reliable workflows, calibrated source localisation, auditable quality control, and empirical evidence for improved diagnostic or treatment decisions. The other is naturalistic neuroscience, where wearable measurement can connect neural dynamics to movement, action, and social behaviour without conflating neural activity with movement-related artefacts. Both trajectories depend on a shared engineering stack including magnetic field control, dense spatial sampling, accurate calibration, integrated electronics, artefact suppression, participant comfort, and synchronised behavioural measurement. The next stage of OPM-MEG should be evaluated by clinical utility in specific patient groups, statistically identifiable neural dynamics in behaviourally rich settings, and sufficient system detail for replication across systems and sites.

title: Rapidly Progressive Alzheimer's Disease: Candidate Mechanisms and Diagnostic Challenges.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) usually follows a slowly progressive course, but some patients experience unusually rapid cognitive and functional decline. This clinical phenotype, commonly termed rapidly progressive Alzheimer's disease (rpAD), has no consensus definition; its status as a distinct biological entity remains unresolved, and its reported frequency depends strongly on operational criteria and referral settings. To synthesize current evidence, we conducted targeted literature searches (up to August 31, 2026) of clinical, neuropathological, and biomarker studies. This narrative review extends earlier overviews by integrating newer genetic, tau-seeding, and blood-biomarker findings with conflicting clinical evidence, while distinguishing candidate mechanisms from established diagnostic tools. Selected autopsy and biomarker studies suggest differences in amyloid-β and tau conformations, synaptic and mitochondrial proteins, neuroinflammatory responses, and concomitant pathologies; however, most data are associative, derive from small or selected cohorts, and do not establish rpAD as a discrete disease subtype. In practice, evaluation should confirm AD pathology while promptly excluding treatable causes and rapidly progressive mimics, particularly Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), using established tools such as cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, MRI, and PrP RT-QuIC. Cerebrospinal fluid, molecular imaging, structural MRI, and emerging blood biomarkers can provide supportive evidence, but no biomarker profile has been prospectively validated as an rpAD-specific diagnostic rule. Harmonized definitions and prospective, biomarker-stratified multicenter validation are required before candidate mechanisms or biomarkers can guide rpAD-specific interventions.

title: Discovery of a Peripherally Directed CB1 Receptor Antagonist That Restores Insulin Signaling in Adipocytes.
abstract: The antagonism of cannabinoid 1 receptor (CB1R) signaling has demonstrated clinical efficacy in treating obesity, improving insulin resistance, enhancing cardiovascular health, and mitigating metabolic risk factors in humans. Despite these positive outcomes, the clinical use of rimonabant was limited by severe central nervous system adverse effects, which reduced interest in CB1R and hindered the exploration of new therapeutic opportunities. Selective targeting of peripheral CB1R represents a promising strategy to overcome these limitations, creating therapeutic opportunities not only for obesity and metabolic disorders but also for smoking and alcohol addiction. Herein, we report a library of 53 novel, potent, and subtype-selective CB1R antagonists bearing polar groups, designed through convergent Ugi-based synthetic pathways. This approach enabled the identification of key structure-activity relationship features within this series and the effective modulation of molecular properties governing blood-brain barrier permeability. Among the compounds evaluated, the piperazine-1-ium derivative 24a stands out as the first permanently charged CB1R antagonist, exhibiting nanomolar affinity (K i = 115 nM) and high CB1R/CB2R selectivity with a favorable physicochemical profile consistent with peripheral restriction and limited blood-brain barrier penetration. Importantly, 24a exhibits robust functional activity in a biologically relevant model of metabolic dysfunction. In insulin-resistant, lipid-hypertrophied adipocytes, 24a restores insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation and significantly enhances lipolytic activity, with effects comparable or superior to those of rimonabant at equivalent concentrations. These findings establish 24a as a promising peripherally restricted CB1R antagonist with demonstrated functional efficacy in a metabolic disease-relevant cellular model.

title: Cortical microinfarcts are associated with thalamic subregional volume and cognitive impairment in small vessel disease.
abstract: Cortical cerebral microinfarcts (CMIs) are small but could induce tissue injury extending beyond the lesion core. The thalamus, as a central cortico-subcortical hub, may be particularly vulnerable to CMI-related remote injury, potentially linking focal cortical lesions to cognitive impairment in cerebral small vessel disease (SVD). We examined associations of CMI burden with thalamic atrophy and cognitive impairment in SVD patients. This cross-sectional study included 133 patients with SVD. CMI burden was visually rated for presence and count. Thalamic volumes were derived from T1 images, and cognition was measured via the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). Linear regression analyses were performed to examine the associations of CMI count with conventional SVD imaging markers, thalamic volumes, and MMSE scores. Exploratory statistical mediation analysis examined the indirect association of CMI count with MMSE via intralaminar thalamic volume. Among 133 participants, 65 had CMIs. Higher CMI count was associated with lower MMSE scores after adjustment for age, sex, educational level, vascular risk factors, and conventional SVD MRI markers (p<0.001). Higher CMI count was not associated with total thalamic volume, but was selectively associated with lower intralaminar thalamic volume (FDR-adjusted p=0.045). The indirect association was statistically significant in the full sample but not after excluding thalamic lacunes. CMIs were associated with cognitive impairment and lower intralaminar thalamic volume. The indirect association should be considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating. These findings highlight the role of the thalamus, as a key cortico-subcortical connectivity hub, in CMI-related remote tissue injury and cognitive dysfunction in SVD.

title: Decoding Parkinson's disease: a systematic review of qEEG biomarkers across clinical domains.
abstract: This systematic review synthesized evidence on quantitative EEG (qEEG) correlates of Parkinson's disease (PD) across five domains: cognition, motor function, pharmacological interventions, neuromodulation, and sleep/non-motor features, evaluating qEEG's potential as a biomarker across these clinical domains. Following PRISMA, we searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus for studies published from 1991 to 2025. We included studies with ≥10 idiopathic PD patients, resting-state qEEG, and empirical data. Methodological quality was assessed using JBI checklists and AMSTAR. We included 89 studies.
