Spectral slowing - reduced posterior dominant frequency and increased theta power - was the most consistent correlate of cognitive impairment. Connectivity measures (PLV, graph metrics) showed stronger associations with motor dysfunction, gait impairment, and freezing than spectral power alone. qEEG changed with dopaminergic drugs (increased alpha/beta) and neuromodulation (DBS, tDCS, rTMS, neurofeedback). Sleep studies revealed spindle density reductions linked to dementia risk. qEEG is a promising biomarker for PD, with distinct electrophysiological correlates across cognitive, motor, pharmacological, and neuromodulatory domains. However, methodological standardization is needed before clinical use. With standardized protocols and multicenter validation, qEEG could aid diagnosis, progression tracking, and personalized therapy in PD.

title: Photobiomodulation as a regulator of neuroinflammation: mechanistic insights and therapeutic potential in brain disorders.
abstract: Brain disorders, including neurodegenerative, neuropsychiatric, and cerebrovascular diseases, represent a growing global health challenge contributing to disability and mortality worldwide. Although these conditions differ in etiology and clinical presentation, accumulating evidence identifies neuroinflammation as a shared pathological mechanism. Involving microglial activation, astrocytic reactivity, cytokine dysregulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier disruption, it contributes to synaptic dysfunction, neuronal loss, and disease progression, yet therapeutic strategies targeting these processes remain limited. Photobiomodulation (PBM), the therapeutic application of low-intensity red to near-infrared light, has emerged as a neurotechnology capable of modulating biological pathways relevant to neuroinflammation. Preclinical studies suggest that PBM may influence mitochondrial activity through cytochrome c oxidase-mediated mechanisms, enhancing cellular metabolism while regulating reactive oxygen species, inflammatory signaling pathways, and tissue homeostasis. Through these effects, PBM may attenuate neuroinflammatory responses, regulate glial activation, and support neuroprotective processes across multiple neurological models. This narrative review examines evidence supporting neuroinflammation as a common denominator across major brain disorders and explores the biological rationale for PBM as a therapeutic strategy. It summarizes the cellular and molecular basis of PBM, its effects on neuroinflammatory pathways, and preclinical and clinical findings across brain disease models. Preclinical findings consistently support a multi-target anti-inflammatory effect, whereas clinical investigation remains at an early stage, with encouraging results in Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis but mainly negative data on primary outcomes in Parkinson's disease and major depressive disorder. Further research is needed to optimize treatment parameters, clarify mechanisms of action, and determine clinical efficacy across disease contexts.

title: Patient-Informed Biomechanical Modeling Reveals Mechanical Mechanism of Brain Damage in Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus.
abstract: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is a globally growing neurological disorder in older adults that is radiologically characterized by enlargement of ventricles. However, it remains unknown whether ventricular enlargement can produce biomechanical loading large enough to drive brain morphological changes and tissue damage. Here, we develop an anatomically detailed biomechanical model of aging human brain and apply ventricular enlargement using a three-dimensional displacement field derived from MRI of iNPH patients and age-matched controls. The model accurately reproduces radiological markers of iNPH, including Evans index, callosal angle, and high-convexity sulcal narrowing. It further predicts large mechanical strains in the periventricular white matter, particularly within the corona radiata, corpus callosum, and anterior thalamic radiations, tracts consistently implicated in iNPH imaging abnormalities. These findings provide strong evidence that ventricular enlargement induces mechanical strain that contributes to iNPH brain abnormalities, which can potentially be reversed by reducing strain following shunting surgery. The biomechanical brain model forms the foundation of a predictive digital platform and future "digital twin" technology to support diagnosis, patient stratification, and treatment planning in iNPH.

title: Are Incretin Receptor Agonists Psychiatric Drugs: Near-term Opportunity or Creative Superlative?
abstract: Incretin receptor agonists (IRAs), including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and dual/triple receptor co-agonists, have transformed the treatment of obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular disease. Given the extraordinary burden of cardiometabolic comorbidity and excess premature mortality in persons living with psychiatric disorders, IRAs represent a highly relevant and potentially transformative pharmacologic class for this population. Beyond their established metabolic indications, a triangulation of preclinical, neuroimaging, observational, and emerging controlled trial evidence suggests that IRAs may exert direct central nervous system effects-augmenting neurogenesis, neuroplasticity, and functional brain connectivity-that underpin putative psychiatric benefits. Replicated evidence supports effects on alcohol and substance use disorders, and preliminary data indicate benefits in mood and neurocognitive disorders. However, controlled trial evidence remains limited and mixed, and several clinical considerations specific to psychiatric populations-including suicidality surveillance, sarcopenia, constipation risk, drug-drug interactions, and aspiration risk with ketamine-require careful attention. Whether IRAs ultimately meet the evidentiary threshold to be classified as psychiatric drugs remains to be determined by ongoing phase III trials. In the interim, their use for cardiometabolic indications in psychiatric populations is well-justified and may confer meaningful mortality reduction.

title: Therapeutic Potential of Classical Psychedelics and Non-Hallucinogenic Psychoplastogens in Psychiatric Disorders.
abstract: Major depressive disorder remains a leading cause of disability worldwide, and current antidepressants are limited by delayed onset and incomplete response. Building on advances driven by ketamine research, renewed interest has focused on classical serotonergic psychedelics-particularly psilocybin, N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT), 5-methoxy-DMT, and lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD)-which, under supervised conditions, can produce rapid and sometimes durable improvements in mood. This review synthesizes contemporary clinical evidence for classical psychedelics in depression and related disorders and evaluates key translational challenges, including small sample sizes, expectancy effects, and limitations in maintaining blinding in randomized controlled trials. We further evaluate mechanistic frameworks that move beyond an exclusively 5-HT2A receptor-centric framework. Classical psychedelics engage multiple serotonergic receptor subtypes and convergent intracellular signaling pathways that modulate glutamatergic neurotransmission, promote synaptic plasticity, and reorganize large-scale brain networks. Converging preclinical and clinical evidence implicates neurotrophic mechanisms-particularly brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) signaling-as contributors to sustained therapeutic effects. Although acute mystical-type experiences may enhance clinical response, emerging evidence suggests they are not strictly required, raising the possibility that plasticity-promoting mechanisms can be partially dissociated from hallucinogenic effects. We also consider peripheral contributions, including gut-brain axis interactions, that may influence treatment durability. Finally, we discuss safety considerations and future directions, emphasizing the need for rigorously designed trials of next-generation non-hallucinogenic psychoplastogens to improve safety, scalability, and long-term tolerability.

title: Management of acute situations in institutionalised Parkinsonian patients: A survey in Seine-Saint-Denis, France.
abstract: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) or atypical parkinsonian syndromes (PS) living in long-term care facilities face complex medical needs, yet little is known about their medical follow-up and reasons for emergency department referrals and hospitalisations in this setting. This study aimed to describe the prevalence of PD/PS among residents of long-term care facilities (EHPADs) in the French Seine-Saint-Denis department, their medical follow-up, and the frequency and reasons for emergency department referrals and hospitalisations. This retrospective study covered the year 2023. All 66 EHPADs in the department were contacted to complete a facility-level questionnaire on PD/PS prevalence and emergency referrals. Facilities with PD/PS residents were then invited to complete a patient-level questionnaire collecting demographic, clinical and follow-up data, and details regarding emergency referrals and hospitalisations. Thirty-five EHPADs (53%) responded, representing 3398 residents. Thirty facilities reported 144 residents with PD or PS, corresponding to a prevalence of 4.24% [95% CI: 3.60-4.98%]. Sixteen (53.3%) EHPADs reported at least one PD/PS resident referred to the emergency department, resulting in 62 referrals during the year, corresponding to an incidence rate of 0.43 [95% CI: 0.33-0.55] referrals per PD/PS resident-year. Eight EHPADs (26.7%) completed the patient-level questionnaire, providing data on 34 residents (median [Q1-Q3] age: 80 [75-85], 73.5% with PD). Over one-third (38.2%) did not have a designated neurologist during 2023. Nine patients (27.3%) were referred to the emergency department, mainly for axial disorders (33.3%) and infections (33.3%). Nine patients (26.5%) were hospitalised. Exploratory analyses showed that hospitalisation was significantly associated with emergency referral (P=0.02) and a last general practitioner consultation that was less often for routine care (P=0.048). PD and PS were frequently identified among residents of participating EHPADs, yet a substantial proportion of patients lack neurological follow-up. Emergency referrals and hospitalisations affected approximately one-quarter of patients, often for potentially preventable causes. These findings suggest that preventive strategies, multidisciplinary follow-up, and improved access to neurologists may help reduce avoidable hospitalisations.

title: Biological mechanisms of ageing and potential therapeutic targets.
Neuron-specific Drp1 deletion exacerbates hippocampal synaptic dysfunction and spatial memory impairment during high-fat diet-induced metabolic stress.
abstract: High-fat diet (HFD)-induced metabolic dysfunction is associated with hippocampal injury and cognitive impairment, but the neuronal factors that determine susceptibility to these abnormalities remain unclear. Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) is a key regulator of mitochondrial fission that supports neuronal and synaptic function. Here, we investigated whether neuron-specific Drp1 deletion aggravates hippocampal dysfunction in mice exposed to an HFD for 6 months. HFD feeding induced metabolic abnormalities. Compared with HFD-fed wild-type mice, HFD-fed neuron-specific Drp1 knockout (Drp1cKO) mice showed lower brain weight and greater spatial-memory impairment. In the hippocampus, Drp1cKO was associated with reduced CA1 mushroom-spine density, lower synapsin1, Homer1, and glutaminase1 levels, and fewer ultrastructurally identifiable synapses. Whole-cell recordings from CA1 pyramidal neurons revealed larger evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents, a lower paired-pulse ratio, and altered input resistance in HFD-fed Drp1cKO mice, whereas resting membrane potential was unchanged. HFD-fed Drp1cKO mice also showed increased TUNEL-positive cells and ProteoStat signal, accompanied by reactive glial alterations in the hippocampus, including reduced microglial ramification and changes in GFAP, galectin-3, and Iba-1 expression. In primary hippocampal neurons, Drp1 knockdown reduced cell viability, increased LDH release and mitochondrial superoxide-associated fluorescence, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduced apposed Synapsin I+/Homer1+ puncta under control and high-glucose conditions. Together, these findings indicate that neuronal Drp1 deficiency is associated with mitochondrial abnormalities, synaptic structural and functional alterations, cellular injury, reactive glial changes, and impaired memory during HFD-induced metabolic stress. Maintenance of Drp1-dependent mitochondrial dynamics may contribute to hippocampal resilience under chronic metabolic stress.

title: Differential behavioral effects of systemic oxytocin receptor blockade across social tasks and hierarchical ranks in male mice.
abstract: Oxytocin receptor signaling has been implicated in diverse social behaviors, but whether its behavioral effects depend on social tasks and an individual's position within a hierarchy remains unclear. We examined the effects of systemic administration of L-368,899, a blood-brain barrier-penetrating oxytocin receptor antagonist, across four domains of social behavior in male C57BL/6 J mice: social rank, sex preference, general social preference, and dyadic interaction. Following the establishment of stable hierarchies in the tube test, administration of L-368,899 (10 mg/kg, intraperitoneally) to first-ranked mice did not alter their hierarchical position. Rank fluctuations were observed more frequently when the antagonist was administered to second-ranked mice. In both rank conditions, the remaining cage mates received saline. In the sex-preference task, saline-treated males spent more time in the female stimulus zone than in the male stimulus zone, whereas this preference was not statistically detectable following treatment with L-368,899 (3 or 10 mg/kg). In contrast, L-368,899 did not significantly alter proximity-based preference for a novel male over a nonsocial object or affect contact duration and inter-individual distance during dyadic interactions between familiar male cage mates, in which both members of each pair received the same treatment. Thus, systemic oxytocin receptor blockade did not produce a generalized reduction in social approach. Instead, the observed behavioral patterns suggest that its effects depend on specific social behavioral tasks and hierarchical position. These findings provide a pharmacological basis for further investigation of the task- and rank-dependent contributions of oxytocin receptor signaling to social behavior.

title: Tributyl phosphate disrupts neuronal autophagy: potential involvement of TLR4 in cell and rat models.
abstract: Tributyl phosphate (TBP), a widely used organophosphate ester, exhibits lipophilic characteristics that enable it to cross the blood-brain barrier. Although its neurotoxicity has been confirmed, the underlying molecular pathways remain unclear. This study examined whether TLR4-associated autophagy disruption contributes to TBP-induced neuronal damage. Autophagy was activated with rapamycin (RAPA) and TLR4 was knocked down using siRNA. TBP exposure upregulated TLR4 expression and downregulated autophagy-related markers. Autophagic flux analysis assays using bafilomycin A1 further revealed that TBP impaired autophagosome biogenesis instead of lysosomal dysfunction. Autophagy activation and TLR4 knockdown each partially attenuated TBP-induced oxidative stress, inflammation, and alterations in neuroinjury markers. Moreover, inhibiting TLR4 partially reversed the decrease in autophagy levels caused by TBP. Molecular docking predicted TBP may bind to the TLR4 extracellular domain, providing a testable framework for future validation. These findings identify TLR4-regulated autophagy suppression as a candidate mechanism for TBP neurotoxicity.

title: Surgical Management and Functional Outcomes of Vestibular Schwannoma: A Retrospective Multi-Center Cohort Study in Romania.
Antipsychotic-related brain changes in first-episode psychosis: a systematic review.
abstract: Antipsychotics (APs) induce functional, anatomical, and metabolic brain changes in schizophrenia, but the nature and clinical significance of these effects remain debated. Focusing on first-episode psychosis (FEP) allows distinction between medication-induced and illness-related brain changes and facilitates identification of early predictors of treatment response. Following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD42021240369), we systematically reviewed longitudinal neuroimaging studies in FEP with the objective of 1) identifying APs-induced brain changes, 2) identifying brain changes associated with clinical improvement, and 3) exploring the potential of neuroimaging biomarkers to predict treatment response. Eighty-six studies were included: 26 structural, 27 functional, and 16 metabolic, including 33 studies specifically addressing predictive biomarkers of treatment response. Across modalities, APs induced measurable brain changes within days to weeks of treatment Ainitiation, particularly in the striatum, thalamus, and prefrontal cortex (PFC), key regions of the striato-thalamo-cortical network. Increased basal ganglia gray matter volume was the most consistent anatomical finding; cortical findings, particularly in the PFC, were more heterogeneous, with both increases and decreases in thickness reported across studies. Functionally, APs normalized abnormal striatal activity and connectivity, correlating with improvement in positive symptoms. In contrast, no reliable imaging correlate has been identified for changes in negative or cognitive symptoms. Metabolic studies showed increased N-acetylaspartate in the thalamus and PFC and normalization of glutamate levels in associative and limbic regions. Baseline brain characteristics, particularly less severe structural or functional abnormalities in the striatum and anterior cingulate cortex, predicted better outcomes. Together, these findings suggest that APs primarily act through modulation and normalization of striato-cortical circuits, with preserved neuroplasticity favoring recovery. Integrating multimodal neuroimaging and computational approaches may advance biomarker-based, individualized treatment strategies in early psychosis.

title: Obesity Paradox and Non-Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Risk.
Current development of therapeutic strategies for Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease is an increasingly prevalent neurodegenerative cause of dementia. The prevailing model begins with neuronal deposits of beta-amyloid (Aβ42) (phase I), followed by intra-neuronal fibrillary tangles of p-tau (phase II) that recruit numerous effector pathways (phase III) leading to neuronal damage, synaptic loss and gliosis. Monoclonal anti-Aβ antibodies and tau substituent peptide-elicited anti-p-tau antibodies reduce brain loads of these pathogenic proteins. Anti-Aβ antibodies decreased cognitive loss by a mean of 26%, but anti-p-tau antibodies had no effect. Anti-p-tau antibodies were well-tolerated, but 30% of patients receiving anti-Aβ antibodies had brain areas of swelling and hemorrhages detected by imaging. Early studies of pharmacological alteration of phase III neuropathic effector mechanisms in humans and mouse models include inhibition of intersectin-1 to preserve mitophagy and synaptic vesicle recycling, melanin-concentrating hormone prevention of memory loss, chimeric (brain astrocyte) antigen-astrocyte reduction in Aβ load, PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitor suppression of neuroinflammation, and reduction in oxidative stress by phytochemicals or MitoVitE. The many possible mechanisms of decreased resilience of neurons to effector attacks of Alzheimer's disease remain under investigation.

title: Beyond the resting ECG: Towards a more personalized approach to cardiovascular screening in elite athletes.
Feasibility of an 8-week lifestyle intervention combining exercise, diet, cognitive training, and social engagement in individuals with mild cognitive impairment: a pilot randomized controlled trial.
abstract: To evaluate the feasibility and preliminary effects of an 8-week multidomain lifestyle intervention for individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). This pilot randomized controlled trial enrolled 30 individuals with MCI who were randomly assigned to a multidomain lifestyle intervention group or a health education control group. The intervention integrated nutritional modification, structured physical exercise, cognitive training, and social engagement over 8 weeks. Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, retention, adherence, and intervention-related adverse events. Exploratory outcomes were assessed at baseline and week 8 including cognitive function, social support, depressive symptoms and health-related quality of life. The recruitment rate was 56.7%, and 78.9% of eligible individuals who were approached provided informed consent. Retention was 100% in both groups, and adherence was high across the intervention components. Although no significant within-group change in cognitive function was observed in the intervention group, a significant between-group difference was detected at post-intervention (P＜0.05). Compared with the control group, the intervention group also showed greater improvement in social support and quality of life, while depressive symptoms were maintained rather than worsening (P＜0.05). This 8-week multidomain lifestyle intervention was feasible and well tolerated in individuals with MCI. Preliminary between-group results favouring the intervention require confirmation in a larger, adequately powered randomized controlled trial with longer follow-up. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06942780 Registered on April 9, 2025,https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT06942780.

title: SIRT1 Signaling in Alzheimer's Disease: Regulation of Mitochondrial Biogenesis and Therapeutic Implications.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is one of the leading causes of dementia worldwide. Its pathological features include Aβ deposition, Tau hyperphosphorylation, and impaired neuronal energy metabolism, accompanied by persistent oxidative stress. As a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)-dependent deacetylase, sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) is a central regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. This review systematically examines the emerging roles of SIRT1 in regulating these pathological processes in AD, with a particular focus on its regulation of mitochondrial biogenesis. It also delineates the complex regulatory mechanisms governing SIRT1, including NAD+-metabolism-dependent regulation, protein interaction-dependent regulation, post-translational modifications such as ISGylation and nitrosylation, and non-coding RNA-mediated post-transcriptional regulation. In addition, the coordinated influence of upstream activators and downstream effectors is discussed. Impairment of SIRT1-mediated mitochondrial biogenesis may exacerbate neuronal energy deficits and oxidative stress in AD, thereby increasing susceptibility to neurodegeneration. This review further elucidates the molecular mechanisms underlying the SIRT1-mitochondrial biogenesis axis. By integrating upstream activating signals with downstream effectors, SIRT1 creates a permissive regulatory environment for peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α)-driven, mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM)-mediated mitochondrial biogenesis, thereby facilitating quality-controlled renewal of the mitochondrial network. In addition, this review discusses the potential value of dynamic biomarker monitoring following therapeutic targeting of the SIRT1 pathway and summarizes current challenges and future intervention strategies. Targeting SIRT1-mediated mitochondrial biogenesis may provide a promising avenue for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for AD.

title: Nanomedicine for Alzheimer's Disease: A Stage-Matched Framework Integrating Pathological Network Modulation, Blood-Brain Barrier Delivery, and Clinical Translation.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains one of the most difficult neurodegenerative disorders to treat. Therapeutic failure is driven mainly by two barriers: the multifactorial pathological network of AD and the limited access of most therapeutics to the brain imposed by the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Conventional symptomatic drugs and emerging antibody-based therapies provide clinical benefit, but they do not fully address the interacting processes involving amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation, Tau pathology, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and synaptic impairment. In this review, we discuss nanomedicine as an integrated platform for AD intervention. We summarize the major pathological nodes that provide targets for nanomedicine-based therapy and discuss BBB structure and transport mechanisms. We then compare polymeric, inorganic, carbon-based, lipid-based, protein-based, nucleic acid-based, and biomimetic platforms in terms of delivery function, intrinsic bioactivity, pathological modulation, and translational risk. Assisted brain-delivery strategies are also discussed, including focused ultrasound-mediated BBB modulation and intranasal nose-to-brain delivery. We then review clinical-stage AD nanomedicine candidates and summarize the key barriers to their translation. This review integrates stage-dependent pathology, BBB transport, and nanoplatform properties. It proposes a stage-matched framework for preclinical, mild symptomatic, and moderate-severe AD. At each stage, the framework matches active pathological nodes with feasible BBB transport strategies, carrier features, and administration routes. It may guide the development of mechanistically defined, reproducible, and clinically testable nanomedicines.

title: Cognitive decline: A 10-year prospective study in glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and age-related macular degeneration.
journal: Archivos de la Sociedad Espanola de Oftalmologia
abstract: To evaluate the longitudinal association of glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy (DR), and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with 10-year cognitive impairment, defined as a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score <26, as well as to determine the predictive value of self-perceived visual function and retinal structural biomarkers for cognitive impairment. The 25-item Visual Function Questionnaire (VFQ-25) assesses self-perceived visual functioning and its impact on vision-related activities and quality of life. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) is a global cognitive screening test assessing domains including orientation, registration and recall, attention/calculation, and language, whereas the MoCA assesses a broader range of cognitive domains, including executive functions, visuospatial abilities, attention, memory, language, and orientation. Because some MMSE and, particularly, MoCA tasks involve visual or visuospatial components, performance may be influenced by visual impairment; both tests may also be influenced by educational level. This monocentric prospective observational study included 360 adults aged ≥60 years (90 participants per group and 90 matched controls) followed for 10 years. Demographic, vascular, and psychosocial variables, best-corrected binocular visual acuity, VFQ-25 (25-item Visual Function Questionnaire), MMSE (Mini-Mental State Examination), and MoCA scores were collected. Retinal structure was assessed using swept-source OCT, including retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) and ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) measurements. Evaluations were performed at baseline, 5 years, and 10 years. Adjusted Cox models, multivariate logistic regression, and longitudinal mixed-effects models were applied. No stratification of glaucoma or diabetic retinopathy according to clinical severity or stage was performed. Cognitive impairment was more frequent in DR (54%), glaucoma (52%), and AMD (49%) compared with controls (27%) (p < 0.001). All ocular diseases remained independently associated with cognitive impairment after multivariate adjustment, with the highest risk observed in DR (HR 2.05). Higher VFQ-25 scores were associated with a lower risk of cognitive impairment, whereas GCIPL thinning showed an independent association with increased risk. However, participants with ocular disease had lower educational attainment, a higher prevalence of depression, and a higher comorbidity index at baseline than controls, and these baseline differences may contribute to the observed associations. Chronic ocular diseases are associated with a higher 10-year risk of cognitive impairment. These findings should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously because of baseline imbalances in education, depression, and comorbidity, the potential influence of visual impairment on cognitive testing, the lack of severity stratification for glaucoma and DR, and the possibility of residual confounding and reverse causality. Self-perceived visual function and retinal structural biomarkers may represent indicators of neurocognitive vulnerability in aging.

title: A three-hit sequential model of chemo-brain: from peripheral inflammation to central oxidative stress and synaptic dysfunction.
abstract: Chemotherapy-induced central neurotoxicity (CICN), commonly known as "chemo-brain", is a prevalent and debilitating condition in cancer survivors, characterized by persistent cognitive deficits that severely compromise quality of life. Despite extensive research, the pathophysiology of CICN remains fragmented, lacking a unifying model that explains how it progresses from peripheral insult to chronic cognitive consolidation. This review proposes a novel Three-Hit sequential model to reconceptualize CICN as a dynamic, staged pathological continuum. Unlike existing multi-hit hypotheses that largely describe cumulative or concurrent CNS risk factors, the Three-Hit model features a therapy-triggered, outside-in cascade with defined temporal checkpoints. The model aims to unify disparate mechanistic findings, explain the enduring nature of cognitive deficits after treatment cessation, and guide stage-specific, mechanism-based precision interventions. The model delineates three sequential pathological phases. The First Hit (peripheral priming) involves chemotherapy-induced gut dysbiosis and systemic inflammation. The Second Hit (central amplification) entails blood-brain barrier disruption, microglial activation, and oxidative stress-driven synaptic dysfunction. The Third Hit (network consolidation) is defined by epigenetic reprogramming, cellular senescence, and white matter degradation, which collectively solidify chronic cognitive impairment. This staged model may facilitate the design of phase-targeted interventions, including microbiota modulation (First Hit), anti-inflammatory and BBB-stabilizing agents (Second Hit), and senotherapeutics or HDAC6 inhibitors (Third Hit), and may guide neuroprotective strategies toward better-timed application. By linking mechanistic insights to a staged biomarker ecosystem, this review offers a conceptual roadmap for advancing stage-specific therapies for CICN.

title: Methadone induces phospholipidosis and lysosomal dysfunction in astrocytes in vitro and in the developing brain.
abstract: Methadone maintenance therapy is the standard treatment for opioid dependence during pregnancy, as its long half-life helps prevent relapse to short-acting abused opioids. However, the cellular mechanisms underlying methadone's neurodevelopmental toxicity remain poorly understood. Lipid dysregulation has emerged as a pathological feature in several neurological conditions and may contribute to cognitive impairment in children exposed to methadone in utero. To determine whether methadone exposure alters lipid homeostasis in astrocytes and to assess whether such alterations are associated with cellular dysfunction and inflammatory responses. Primary rat astrocytes were treated with methadone for three days. Lipid accumulation, lipid droplet formation, and lysosomal distribution were assessed using BODIPY-493/503, perilipin-2 immunostaining, and LysoTracker, respectively, followed by confocal microscopy and colocalization analyses. Ultrastructural changes were examined by electron microscopy. Lipid composition was quantified by mass spectrometry-based lipidomics. Findings were validated in cortical organotypic cultures and in the cortex of pups born to methadone-exposed dams using RT-qPCR, immunofluorescence, and ultrastructural analyses. Translational relevance was further assessed in primary human fetal astrocytes. Methadone exposure induced a dose and time-dependent accumulation of lysosomal lipids in primary neonatal rat astrocytes, independent of lipid droplet formation and opioid receptor activation. Electron microscopy revealed multilamellar bodies characteristic of drug-induced phospholipidosis, a known effect of many cationic amphiphilic drugs. Lipidomics confirmed elevated levels of ceramides and triglycerides. Methadone-treated astrocytes displayed impaired lysosomal degradation capacity, indicating functional compromise. Similar lysosomal and inflammatory alterations were observed in methadone-exposed organotypic cultures and in the cortex of offspring from methadone-treated dams. Human fetal astrocytes replicated these findings, demonstrating cross-species conservation. Methadone induces phospholipidosis and lysosomal dysfunction in astrocytes, accompanied by neuroinflammatory activation during brain development. These findings uncover an unrecognized mechanism linking methadone's amphiphilic properties to developmental neurotoxicity and emphasize the need to re-evaluate the safety of methadone use during pregnancy.

title: Harmonization of transdiagnostic psychiatric phenotypes across a large multi-site study reveals high burden of neuropsychiatric multimorbidity in 16p11.2 and 22q11.2 copy number variant carriers.
authors: van den Bree Marianne B M
abstract: Modern psychiatric research is increasingly collaborative, but significant differences in recruitment and assessment methods across cohorts present major methodological challenges when integrating data. The Core Psychiatric Phenotype Summary (C2PS) tool was developed to harmonize data on psychiatric/neurodevelopmental diagnoses and subthreshold symptoms from multiple sources. Demonstrating its reliability, and breadth and depth, we report findings in the largest cohort to date of individuals with reciprocal copy number variants (CNVs) at 22q11.2 or 16p11.2, collected across 14 international sites in the Genes to Mental Health (G2MH) Network. Neuropsychiatric phenotypes were harmonized for 1,325 G2MH participants (22qdel: n=752, 22qdup: 219, 16pdel: 227, 16pdup: 127, median age 16.0 years [IQR 11.0, 27.0], 52% female). Inter-rater reliability indicated fair-to-excellent agreement across C2PS domains (Light's Kappa: 0.48 to 1). Completion was feasible, with an average of 4% missingness (range 1% to 13%). Multimorbidity (> 2 disorders) affected 57%, with a median of 3 (IQR: 2 to 5) disorders per individual. Of those without any neuropsychiatric diagnosis (n= 244, 18%), subthreshold symptoms were common (82% in >1 domain, 57% > 2 domains). Higher multimorbidity was associated with lower adaptive functioning on the Vineland Adaptative Behavior Scales [-5.5 points per additional impacted domain (95% CI: -7.5, -3.6; p=5x10-8]. The C2PS is a pragmatic and reliable tool to harmonize heterogeneous neuropsychiatric phenotypic data for large multi-national studies. Observations in 1,325 individuals with CNVs at 16p11.2 or 22q11.2 reveal variant-specific psychiatric profiles, emphasize burden and impact of psychiatric multimorbidity, and provide insights beyond categorical diagnoses.

title: A mechanistic analysis of primary neurons from a maternal immune activation model of schizophrenia reveals complex I dysfunction and mitochondrial-driven neurodevelopmental deficits.
abstract: Maternal immune activation (MIA) is a major environmental risk factor for schizophrenia, yet the early neuronal mechanisms linking embryonic immune challenges to neurodevelopmental disruption remain poorly defined. Here, we provide a detailed mechanistic characterization of primary cortical neurons derived from a Poly(I:C)-induced MIA model, revealing mitochondrial dysfunction as a central feature of the pathological phenotype. Cortical neurons cultured from the offspring of Poly(I:C)-treated females (embryonic day 14) exhibited a severely constrained bioenergetic state, characterized by increased basal respiration and ATP levels coupled with a significant reduction in both maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity, indicating limited metabolic flexibility. This bioenergetic failure was accompanied by elevated mitochondrial superoxide production, consistent with a sustained redox imbalance. Concomitant alterations in mitochondrial proteins, including a marked reduction in NDUFS2 levels, further support the involvement of respiratory chain Complex I instability. Moreover, mitochondrial dynamics and content were profoundly disrupted, as evidenced by dysregulated OPA1, DRP1, and TOM20/TOM40 expression, which correlated with a reduced functional pool and a maladaptive remodeling toward enlarged, rounded, or fragmented mitochondria. Notably, these mitochondrial deficits directly paralleled a simplified dendritic arborization and impaired synaptic organization, thereby linking early bioenergetic and redox disturbances to structural neuronal impairments. Collectively, our findings identify mitochondrial dysfunction as a key mechanistic axis connecting prenatal inflammation to neurodevelopmental vulnerability, offering a cell-autonomous framework for how gestational immune challenges translate into structural deficits relevant to schizophrenia.

title: Maternal immune activation and the dopaminergic system: Models, mechanisms, and links to psychiatric disorders.
abstract: Maternal immune activation (MIA) during pregnancy, triggered by infectious or non-infectious factors, is a significant risk factor for neurodevelopmental disorders such as schizophrenia (SZ) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), which are associated with dysfunctions of the dopaminergic system. Animal models using immune challenges like LPS and Poly(I:C) during gestation recapitulate key behavioral and neurochemical phenotypes observed in these disorders. This review synthesizes current evidence from both human epidemiological studies and animal models, highlighting the links between prenatal inflammation and alterations in dopaminergic circuits. In animal models, MIA causes region-specific changes in dopamine (DA) metabolism, receptor expression, and dopaminergic neuron activity. Notably, hyperdopaminergic states in the striatum and hypodopaminergic states in the cortex have been reported in animal models of MIA, but with some variability across studies. Surprisingly, decreased activity of ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopaminergic neurons in vivo emerges as one of the most robust findings in animal models of MIA. We discuss the possible mechanisms underlying MIA-induced dopaminergic phenotypes, focusing in particular on the endocannabinoid system and on microglia-mediated synaptic refinement and complement system activation. This review underscores the complexity of MIA's impact on brain development and dopaminergic function, emphasizing the need for further research into region-specific mechanisms underlying neuropsychiatric vulnerability, as well as innovative methodologies to investigate how MIA leads to long-term changes in the dynamics of DA release in behaving animals.

title: microRNA-Loaded Extracellular Vesicles: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential in Senescence and Ageing.
abstract: Cellular senescence is a biological process characterized by stable cell cycle arrest that contributes to tumor suppression and tissue remodeling but can also promote aging-associated dysfunction when senescent cells persist and accumulate. Senescent cells influence neighboring and distant tissues through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), of which extracellular vesicles (EVs) are an increasingly recognized component. This review examines how microRNAs (miRNAs) carried by EVs regulate senescence and ageing. miRNAs are key post-transcriptional regulators of senescence, particularly within the p53/p21Cip1 and p16INK4a/Rb tumor suppressor pathways. Selective sorting into EVs allows these molecules to act over long distances. EV-miRNAs have dual roles: anti-senescent miRNAs such as miR-17-5p, miR-146a and miR-378a-3p promote rejuvenation, whereas pro-senescent miRNAs including miR-34a, miR-21 and miR-27a propagate ageing. Hypothalamic neural stem cell-derived miRNAs maintain transcriptional homeostasis and suppress senescence across the brain, and their age-related decline contributes to neurodegeneration. miRNAs in small EVs from young plasma rejuvenate multiple organ systems and extend lifespan in mice, while adipocyte-derived miR-27a spreads metabolic dysfunction to distant tissues. Together, EV-miRNAs are an emerging component of the intercellular networks regulating cellular senescence and aging, and their selective sorting, intercellular transfer, and modulation of senescence-associated pathways provide opportunities for therapeutic development and biomarker discovery.

title: Brain metabolomics reveals metabolic alterations associated with chronic polystyrene microplastic-induced neurotoxicity in Drosophila melanogaster.
abstract: Microplastic (MP) pollution is a widespread global environmental problem and poses growing risks to food safety and human health. Increasing evidence indicates that MPs accumulate in human biological tissues, including the brain. However, the brain-specific metabolic alterations associated with chronic MPs exposure remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the neurotoxic effects of chronic dietary exposure to polystyrene microplastics (PS-MPs; 10 and 50 ppm) in Drosophila melanogaster using an integrated metabolomic, biochemical, histological, and behavioral approach. Chronic dietary exposure to PS-MPs is linked to behavioral impairments, including decreased locomotor activity, impaired climbing, altered feeding, and reduced circadian amplitude, at the two tested concentrations. Untargeted brain metabolomics revealed widespread alterations in amino acid, nitrogen, kynurenine, polyamine, and central carbon metabolism, including reduced putrescine, elevated spermidine and spermine, and perturbations in glycolytic and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates. Biochemical analyses demonstrated elevated oxidative stress and impaired antioxidant defenses, including reduced catalase (↓46%) and superoxide dismutase (↓40%) activity, and evidence of mitochondrial impairment (increased mitochondrial ROS, loss of membrane potential, reduced electron transport, altered NAD/NADH balance, and diminished metabolic viability). Histological examination revealed increased brain tissue damage and decreased neuronal viability. Moreover, PS-MPs exposure was associated with alterations in dopaminergic markers, including reduced tyrosine hydroxylase and dopamine levels, together with decreased γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), indicating broader neurotransmitter alterations. These findings show that chronic PS-MPs exposure is associated with widespread brain metabolic perturbations, mitochondrial dysfunction, and dopaminergic impairment, highlighting associations between chronic PS-MPs exposure, brain metabolic alterations, and neurotoxic outcomes.

title: Single-Nucleus RNA Sequencing Analysis of the MECP2-Deficient Marmoset Hippocampus Reveals Altered Maturation-Associated Transcriptional Programs in Hippocampal Granule Neurons.
abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder primarily caused by mutations in the methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene. Although rodent models have provided important insights into RTT pathogenesis, the cell type-specific consequences of MECP2 deficiency in the primate brain remain poorly understood. Here, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing of the hippocampus from MECP2-deficient common marmosets to characterize transcriptional alterations associated with RTT. Analysis of hippocampal nuclei identified major neuronal and glial populations, including the dentate gyrus neurogenic lineage. In the MECP2-deficient hippocampus, immature and mature granule neurons displayed the most pronounced abnormalities, whereas neural stem cells and neural progenitors exhibited relatively limited transcriptional changes. Differential expression and functional enrichment analyses revealed disruption of synaptic signaling, neuronal communication, and circuit organization pathways, accompanied by altered developmental programs. Co-expression network analysis identified maturation-associated modules and hub genes, including GABBR2, NRXN3, and NRG3. Astrocytes and microglia/macrophages also exhibited transcriptional alterations associated with metabolic, lipid-remodeling, phagocytic, and immune-related processes. Cross-species comparison with published Mecp2-mutant mouse dentate gyrus datasets identified a limited but biologically relevant set of shared transcriptional alterations, particularly among downregulated genes involved in synaptic and neuronal functions. These findings indicate that MECP2 deficiency preferentially alters maturation-associated transcriptional programs and synaptic network programs in granule neurons in the primate hippocampus and support partial conservation of abnormalities across rodent and primate RTT models.

title: Pediatric Retinal Disorders.
abstract: Pediatric retinal disorders consist of a plethora of pathophysiologies that directly impact the retinal structure and function, thereby compromising children's vision and quality of life. These disorders can affect children's vision in a wide range of diseases, from minor visual acuity deficits to total vision loss. This review aims to highlight the characteristics and management of pediatric retinal disorders for practicing pediatricians and other primary care clinicians.

title: Association of HPV/p16 status with post-test disease risk after [18F]FDG PET/CT in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Post-treatment [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography ([18F]FDG PET/CT) guides response assessment after definitive (chemo)radiotherapy for oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC), but its clinical meaning may differ by human papillomavirus (HPV)/p16 status. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through 14 July 2026 for studies reporting post-treatment PET/CT outcomes with HPV/p16 information. Early residual disease, later failure or recurrence, equivocal findings, second-look PET/CT, and later surveillance were analysed separately. Internal HPV/p16-stratified comparisons were pooled as random-effects risk ratios with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman confidence intervals. Thirty-three reports, representing approximately 24 cohort families, were included; three predominantly OPSCC cohorts contributed to the primary comparison. After a positive or less-than-complete first PET/CT, subsequent disease risk was not demonstrably different between HPV/p16-positive and HPV/p16-negative disease (risk ratio 0.53, 95 % confidence interval 0.08-3.38; I2 = 75.8 %). After a negative or complete-response scan, risk was lower in HPV/p16-positive disease (risk ratio 0.23, 95 % confidence interval 0.07-0.74; I2 = 0 %). Early studies consistently reported high negative predictive values but heterogeneous positive predictive values. Event rates after equivocal findings ranged from 11.8 % to 72.7 %. In selected cohorts, 30.7-70.7 % of incomplete responses converted to complete metabolic response on second-look PET/CT. HPV/p16 status appeared to modify post-test risk more consistently than intrinsic PET discrimination. Negative scans were associated with lower subsequent disease risk in HPV/p16-positive OPSCC. Given the few direct comparisons and heterogeneous methods, positive or equivocal findings require cautious, context-specific interpretation; fixed HPV/p16-specific management algorithms are not supported.

title: Higher fitness levels associate with higher brain volume and lower lesion volume in youth with Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: To determine relationships between cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) and brain volumetrics in youth with Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Cardiopulmonary exercise testing, physical activity (PA) metrics and MRI lesion/brain volumetrics were obtained on youth with MS (n = 33; 26F; median age 16.5years; IQR 1.91). Pearsons' correlations were used to assess the relationships between lesion/brain volume, cardiorespiratory fitness and physical activity. We found associations between: (1) higher lesion volume and lower workload-max z-scores (r=-0.35, p = 0.04); (2) whole brain and thalamic volumes and VO2 peak (r = 0.55, p > 0.001; r = 0.41, p = 0.018) and maximum workload (whole brain volume, r = 0.45, p = 0.009); (3) VO2 peak and hippocampal dentate gyrus head volume (r = 0.36, p = 0.04). Higher CRF, but not PA levels, were associated with lower lesion volumes and greater whole brain, thalamic and dentate gyrus volume in youth with MS. Future studies using longitudinal and interventional designs are needed to establish the directionality of these relationships.

title: Cognitive resilience and improvements in health-related quality of life over 4 years in people with relapsing multiple sclerosis treated with cladribine tablets: Results from the CLARIFY-MS Extension study.
abstract: The initial 2-year phase 4 CLARIFY-MS Parent study demonstrated improvements in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and preserved cognitive function in cladribine tablets (CladT)-treated people with highly active relapsing multiple sclerosis (RMS). To report 4-year data on cognitive function, HRQoL, other efficacy and safety outcomes from CLARIFY-MS Extension. No additional CladT treatment was protocolled during Extension (as per approved EU label). The primary endpoint was the proportion of participants with no or minimal decline in cognitive function at Month (M) 48 after initial dose versus Parent study baseline. HRQoL, and other efficacy and safety outcomes of CladT were also assessed. Overall, 68.6% of the participants (n = 192/280) showed no or minimal decline in cognitive function at M48 versus Parent study baseline. Significant improvements in Multiple Sclerosis Quality of Life-54 scores were observed over 48 months. The beneficial effect of CladT on relapses, radiological activity and disability progression observed in the Parent study were sustained during Extension. No unexpected safety signals were detected. CLARIFY-MS Extension demonstrated sustained benefits of CladT on cognitive function and HRQoL in people with highly active RMS for ≤4 years after the initial dose. The 4-year follow-up of the BICAMS battery indicated resilience across different aspects of cognition with CladT. The durable and multidimensional effects of CladT on key efficacy outcomes observed during the 2-year treatment-period of the Parent study were confirmed over the treatment-free Years 3-4 of Extension. The existing safety profile of CladT was confirmed over 4 years. CLARIFY-MS Extension study: URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04776213; clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT04776213.

title: Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including Lower Extremities (HABIT-ILE) in adults with chronic stroke: a randomized controlled trial.
journal: Annals of physical and rehabilitation medicine
abstract: Stroke rehabilitation guidelines recommend goal-oriented, task-specific, intensive interventions. Yet most programs emphasize upper extremity (UE) recovery, overlooking lower extremities (LEs) and trunk, which are essential for activities of daily living. Consequently, Hand-Arm Bimanual Intensive Therapy Including LEs (HABIT-ILE) represents a promising approach for stroke rehabilitation. This randomized controlled trial aimed to determine the effect of HABIT-ILE and to compare its efficacy with a control group in adults with chronic hemiparetic stroke by promoting greater improvements across the body functions, activity, and participation domains of the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health. Forty-six adults with hemiparetic chronic stroke were randomized to either a 2-week (50 h, 5 h/day) HABIT-ILE camp-setting program in Brussels, Belgium, or to continue their usual neurorehabilitation (mean = 4 h 36 min) for over the same period. Participants were assessed before, immediately, and at 3 months after intervention using the Adult Assisting Hand Assessment Stroke (Ad-AHA Stroke, primary outcome), the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM), the Fugl Meyer Assessment for UEs (FMA-UE), the Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT), the ABILHAND-CS and ACTIVLIM-CS questionnaires, the six-minute walk test, the modified Rankin Scale and the Stroke Impact Scale (SIS). The ANCOVA revealed a significant between-groups difference favoring the HABIT-ILE group (TG), with a time effect observed for the Ad-AHA Stroke (TG: at 2 weeks = +6.24% of logits; at 3 months = +7.05% of logits), WMFT (Functional Ability Scale, all P ≤ 0.041), and COPM (P < 0.001, performance and satisfaction) at both 2 weeks and 3 months. We found a similar significant effect for the SIS (hand function, P = 0.003) at 2 weeks and the FMA-UE and ABILHAND-CS at 3 months (all P ≤ 0.033). We observed no significant between-group differences for the other outcomes, including LEs measures. In adults with chronic stroke, HABIT-ILE intervention significantly improved spontaneous bimanual use, motor function, and ability of the paretic UE (both externally rated and self-perceived) and reduced participation restrictions compared with the control group. This randomized controlled trial was registered on December 11th, 2020, on ClinicalTrials.gov as "HABIT-ILE in Adults With Chronic Stroke (HABIT-ILE Stroke)", with the registration number NCT04664673 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04664673?cond=NCT04664673&rank=).

title: Calmodulin kinase-like vesicle-associated protein (CAMKV) autoimmune encephalitis: Neurological & oncological accompaniments, treatments & outcomes.
abstract: We previously reported CAMKV-IgG paraneoplastic encephalitis accompanying uterine and neuroendocrine-lineage carcinomas. Here, we describe 7 new cases (12 total) and report CSF cytokine/chemokine profiles and coexisting antibody frequency. Patient samples demonstrating the CAMKV-specific murine tissue-based indirect immunofluorescence assay (TIIFA) staining pattern were tested by protein microarray and confirmed CAMKV-specific cell-based assay. CSF cytokines/chemokines were analyzed in 4 patients. Median symptom-onset age was 69 years (range 53-79); 8/12 were women. Common manifestations included altered mental status (7/12), hyperkinetic movements (6/12), seizures (5/12), psychiatric, and insomnia (4/12 each). Five patients had coexisting antibodies: tripartite motif-containing protein-9 (3), N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (2), antineuronal nuclear antibody-type-1 (ANNA-1) and γ-aminobutyric acid B receptor (1 each). All 12 had cancer, including adenocarcinoma (6/12; uterine 4, lung 1, prostate 1), lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin), or other carcinoma (urothelial, Merkel cell, hepatocellular, and poorly differentiated (1 each). All 3 available cancers (uterine, 2; prostate adenocarcinoma, 1) were immunohistochemistry positive for CAMKV. 6/8 had CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis. MRIs revealed mesial temporal and basal ganglia T2 hyperintensities in 6/10 and 5/10, respectively. Among 7 immunotherapy-treated patients, 6 improved initially, although 5/7 with follow-up died from cancer. CSF IL-13 and GM-CSF were significantly elevated compared with non-inflammatory controls (FDR-adjusted P < 0.05). Four of 42 ANNA-1 positive samples with coexisting synaptic TIIFA staining were CAMKV-IgG positive. CAMKV-IgG is a paraneoplastic encephalitis autoantibody associated with diverse cancers. Neurologic improvement with immunotherapy is frequent, but prognosis is driven by cancer outcomes. Elevated IL-13 may indicate metastatic risk.

title: The impact of diagnostic criteria on the detection of nocturnal hypoventilation in adult amyotrophic lateral sclerosis patients.
abstract: Nocturnal hypoventilation (NH) is an early manifestation of respiratory muscle weakness in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and plays a key role in determining the optimal timing for non-invasive ventilation (NIV). However, several diagnostic definitions of NH have been proposed, and their impact on NH prevalence remains unclear. In this cross-sectional study, 56 non-ventilated ALS patients underwent home-based overnight monitoring with transcutaneous carbon dioxide (TcCO2) and pulse oximetry. NH prevalence was assessed using seven definitions derived from daytime arterial blood gases, nocturnal oximetry, and TcCO2 parameters. Agreement between definitions was evaluated using Cohen's and Light's kappa coefficients. NH prevalence varied widely depending on the definition used, ranging from approximately 5% with daytime arterial criteria to 36.7% using peak TcCO2 ≥49 mmHg. Overall concordance among definitions was low (Light's κ = 0.27), indicating that current NH definitions are not interchangeable. Currently used definitions of NH in ALS show substantial heterogeneity and identify different patient subsets. These findings highlight the need for ALS-specific consensus definitions of NH.

title: Timing matters: Maternal stress and mental health symptoms from pregnancy to postpartum in shaping infant development.
abstract: Maternal perceived stress, mental health, and physiological dysregulation during pregnancy can alter the intrauterine environment, shaping infant development through fetal programming processes. Nonetheless, few longitudinal studies in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) have jointly examined psychological and biological factors in relation to infant outcomes. This longitudinal study followed 146 Pakistani mother-infant dyads at early to mid-gestation (T1), mid- to late gestation (T2), and postpartum (T3). Maternal perceived stress, depressive symptoms, and social support were measured across all timepoints, whereas pregnancy-related anxiety and an allostatic load index of physiological dysregulation were measured during pregnancy. Infant developmental outcomes across five domains were assessed using the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3). Perceived stress at each timepoint, depressive symptoms at T1 and T3, and allostatic load at T1 were associated with poorer infant fine motor skills. Perceived stress at T3 was linked to poorer infant problem solving. Communication, gross motor, and personal-social skills in infants showed no associations. Higher T3 social support attenuated the relationship between prenatal perceived stress and fine motor skills. Moreover, an exploratory interaction showed that T1 allostatic load related to lower fine motor skills when T3 stress is high. Psychological and biological pathways may link maternal prenatal risk to infant fine motor development, with the postpartum environment possibly influencing whether prenatal vulnerabilities translate into delays. Interventions strengthening social resources and reducing postpartum stress may help disrupt intergenerational stress transmission in LMICs.

title: Optimization of [18F]Fallypride synthesis for distribution over long distances.
journal: Applied radiation and isotopes : including data, instrumentation and methods for use in agriculture, industry and medicine
abstract: Specialized radiotracers, especially those that are not FDA approved, are often only available at academic research facilities. This restricts patient demographics and prevents patients from being able to participate or benefit from cutting edge medical advancement. We have developed an optimized method for the synthesis and long-distance shipment of a radiotracer used in clinical research regarding dopamine D2/D3 receptors, [18F]Fallypride. The radiotracer was obtained in 7% n.d.c. radiochemical yield, passed all required QA/QC requirements, and was shipped to a location 7 h drive from the synthesis site. The delivered tracer was used to obtain PET/CT images comparable to a locally made radiotracer.

title: Modulatory effects of marine algae-derived natural products on nervous system.
journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
abstract: The pathological changes in neurodegenerative diseases are complicated and involve oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, protein misfolding, and synaptic loss. Marine algae contain a wide range of diverse natural compounds, such as polysaccharides, phenolics, terpenoids, and pigments, some of which may help preserve neurons by targeting oxidative pathways, dampening inflammatory responses, and preventing toxic protein aggregation. This review aims to recapitulate current advances on the regulatory roles of marine algae-derived natural products on nervous system. In addition, representative compounds are discussed, together with the relationship between their structures and neuroprotective properties. To conduct this structured narrative review, we collected relevant literature obtained from PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar up to June 2026. Relevant studies on the effect of algal products on neuroprotection were selected and articles were searched using terms that covered marine algae, natural products, neurodegenerative diseases, and structure-activity relationship. Natural products found in marine algae may support neuronal protection through the modulation of redox balance, inflammatory signaling, and proteostasis. Their neuroprotective activities are closely associated with structural determinants, and are intrinsically shaped by characteristics like sulfation degree, molecular weight, hydroxyl groups, and conjugated systems. This article underscores the potential of these products for neuroprotective interventions, and further studies are warranted to clarify their bioavailability and clinical efficacy.

title: Biopsychosocial versus purely biological explanation for persistent physical symptoms following COVID-19: An experimental study with lay participants and healthcare professionals.
abstract: This study aims to compare changes of attitudes regarding the causation, evolution, and treatment for persistent physical symptoms following COVID-19 after lay participants and healthcare professionals receive medical explanations presenting either a purely biological or a biopsychosocial account of symptoms. Participants completed an online questionnaire assessing their views on underlying physical and mental causation, chronicity, disability and annoyance of symptoms, required examinations, and appropriate treatments. Lay participants rated their feelings of offence and anxiety associated with symptoms, while healthcare professionals their feelings of competence and willingness to care for a patient with persistent physical symptoms following COVID-19. All participants were allocated alternatingly to watch a standardized video with distinct accounts: either purely biological or biopsychosocial. -tests were used to compare representations after explanations. A total of 208 lay participants (mean age: 42; 74% women) and 104 healthcare professionals (mean age: 42; 68% women) were included. The two explanations were efficient in changing beliefs about mental and physical causation of persistent physical symptoms following COVID-19 in both participants' groups. Compared to the purely biological explanation, the biopsychosocial explanation increased feelings of offence while at the same time decreasing lay participants' views that symptoms are chronic and disabling and increasing views that symptoms can be improved with CBT and physical exercise therapy. In healthcare professionals, the biopsychosocial explanation increased feelings of competence and belief that symptoms can be improved with CBT. A standardized biopsychosocial video explanation may help promoting integrative care. Results suggest that explaining the biopsychosocial approach can modulate healthcare professionals' and lay people's attitudes towards persistent physical symptoms following COVID-19. Future research should investigate how explaining the biopsychosocial approach can be further improved to promote more sustained changes in attitudes over time.

title: NOD1 and neurodegenerative diseases: Exploring the interplay between innate immune signaling and cognitive decline.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are one of the biggest health problems worldwide, but there are no effective disease-modifying therapies available, due to the lack of understanding of the molecular mechanisms involved in chronic neuroinflammation and progressive neuronal loss. There is growing evidence that innate immune dysregulation plays a central role in disease progression, but the role of nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain 1 (NOD1), an intracellular pattern-recognition receptor (PRR), has been understudied. Beyond antimicrobial defense, NOD1 regulates receptor-interacting protein kinase 2 (RIPK2)-dependent nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling and may contribute to neuroinflammatory responses. This review summarizes the structural biology, activation mechanisms, intracellular signaling pathways, and emerging role of NOD1 in neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative diseases. The interaction between NOD1 signaling, the gut-brain axis, and peripheral immune regulation is also discussed, with a focus on how chronic activation of the NOD1-RIPK2 signaling pathway may exacerbate neuroinflammatory responses and influence disease progression. Recent advances in the pharmacological modulation of NOD1, current knowledge gaps, and challenges for clinical translation are also discussed. Altogether, current evidence positions NOD1 as a potential modulator of neuroinflammation and a possible link between innate immune signaling and neurodegeneration, although its role as a primary disease driver remains unestablished. Understanding NOD1-dependent signaling networks may enable targeted immunomodulatory therapies to reduce neuroinflammation and slow neurodegeneration.

title: A practical approach to dietary interventions in pediatric irritable bowel syndrome.
abstract: Pediatric irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a gut-brain axis disorder that negatively affects the quality of life of children and adolescents. Because up to 90% of children and parents report a direct correlation between the consumption of specific foods and symptom exacerbation, dietary intervention is a therapeutic challenge. However, the lack of nutritional guidance leads parents to self-manage their children's diets, thereby increasing the risk of dietary restrictions and nutritional deficiencies. This review analyzes current evidence on dietary therapy for pediatric IBS, focusing on efficacy, safety, and the risk of nutritional deficiencies. Traditional dietary advice is recommended as the first-line dietary approach, promoting a set of lifestyle and dietary recommendations; it demonstrates long-term clinical efficacy comparable to more restrictive diets while minimizing the risk of eating disorders. The Mediterranean diet serves as a protective and sustainable diet, offering anti-inflammatory effects and favorable microbiota modulation by prebiotic fiber and antioxidant compounds. By contrast, the low-fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols diet is reserved for selected cases owing to its restrictive nature and potential for nutritional deficiencies. To date, the gluten-free diet approach remains limited and controversial in children. Moreover, reduction of ultra-processed foods is a further diet strategy for IBS symptoms; ultra-processed foods are often rich in fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, polyols, and added sugars, leading to microbiota dysbiosis and symptom exacerbation. Overall, a multidisciplinary and family-centered approach is essential to control IBS symptoms in children, focusing on personalized diet and behavioral interventions.

title: Imaginal neglect as a disorder of mental scene construction.
journal: Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
abstract: Imaginal (representational) neglect-typically revealed by contralesional omissions when patients describe familiar places from long-term memory-provides a test case for theories of mental scene construction. Unlike propositional recall of place-related facts, imaginal tasks require that semantic knowledge be "spatialized" into a viewpoint-dependent scene that can be actively sampled. We review converging evidence from classic behavioral dissociations (viewpoint inversion; preserved semantic knowledge with impaired spatialized retrieval), oculomotor measures during imagery, sensory interventions (caloric vestibular stimulation; prismatic adaptation), and lesion/disconnection findings. Reconsidering the long-standing opposition between a primary "representational scotoma" and a pure attentional/exploratory bias, we argue that this dichotomy may not correspond to how scenes are actually built: construction and exploration are tightly coupled processes, partly implemented through attentional/oculomotor control. Building on convergent lesion, meta-analytic and neuroimaging evidence that a left-lateralized image-generation system (including the Fusiform Imagery Node) supports the generation of visual content, we propose as a working hypothesis that balanced, viewpoint-dependent spatial organization depends on right-hemisphere attentional control and inter-hemispheric integration, plausibly involving posterior callosal pathways. We specify construction and exploration as sets of operations, relate the framework to accounts of conscious access, and set out empirical tests of its network-level claims.

title: Prevalence and clinical correlates of sleep disturbances in hemifacial spasm: A multi-centre case-control study.
abstract: Hemifacial spasm (HFS) is a chronic movement disorder characterised by involuntary contractions of muscles on one side of the face. While motor features are well recognised, sleep disturbances in HFS have not been studied in detail. We aimed to compare the prevalence of sleep disturbances between HFS patients and healthy controls and examine clinical factors associated with sleep dysfunction in HFS. This cross-sectional case-control study included 133 HFS patients and 227 age- and gender-matched healthy controls. Validated questionnaires were used to assess excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), sleep quality, insomnia, restless legs syndrome (RLS), probable rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder (pRBD), and high risk of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Anxiety, depression, and quality of life were assessed. HFS severity was assessed using the Hemifacial Spasm Grading Scale. Compared to healthy controls, HFS patients had a greater prevalence of EDS (P = 0.003), poor sleep quality (P < 0.001), moderate-to-severe insomnia (P < 0.001), pRBD (P = 0.007), RLS (P < 0.001), high risk for OSA (P = 0.005), depression (P = 0.009), and lower quality of life (P < 0.001). Multivariate analysis showed that poor sleep quality was associated with anxiety; RLS with HFS severity, and high risk for OSA with a higher body mass index (BMI) and hypertension, among patients with HFS. Poor quality of life in HFS was associated with presence of poor sleep quality, pRBD, RLS, anxiety, and depressive symptoms. Sleep disturbances are common in HFS, and are associated with disease severity, high BMI, and anxiety. Sleep and mood symptoms worsen quality of life in these patients.

title: CSF neurofilament, daily function, and survival correlates of a MOBP risk variant in the Barcelona PSP Registry: an exploratory study.
abstract: To investigate whether the PSP risk T-allele of the rs1768208 polymorphism at the MOBP locus is associated with neuroaxonal injury, as reflected by CSF levels of neurofilament light chain (CSF-NfL), and with exploratory clinical outcomes related to disease severity and progression. We included patients from the Barcelona PSP Registry, a longitudinal, multicentre cohort. Participants underwent standardized clinical assessments, genetic testing, CSF-NfL determination, and longitudinal follow-up. Associations between MOBP rs1768208 genotype and CSF-NfL levels were evaluated using multivariable models adjusted for age, sex, and phenotype. Daily functioning (Schwab & England Activities of Daily Living, SEADL) and survival were explored as additional clinical outcomes. Carriers of the rs1768208 T-allele showed higher CSF-NfL levels in a dose-dependent manner and a higher likelihood of exceeding a clinically relevant CSF-NfL cut-off. Exploratory analyses showed associations of rs1768208 T/T homozygosity with worse functional status and shorter survival. This is the first study showing an in vivo association between a PSP genetic risk variant and a biomarker of neuroaxonal injury. Exploratory associations with clinical outcomes are aligned with the NfL association. If further confirmed, these findings could improve biological stratification and inform patient selection for, and interpretation of, clinical trials.

title: Mesenchymal stromal cells for progressive multiple sclerosis: current evidence and translational challenges.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS) characterized by demyelinating lesions leading to cumulative and irreversible neurological damage. In the progressive form of MS (PMS), pathogenic mechanisms are multifaceted, involving both compartmentalized inflammation and neurodegeneration. Owing to their immunomodulatory and trophic properties, mesenchymal stromal cells (MSC) have emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy for this patient population. To review the relevant immunomodulatory and neuroprotective mechanisms of MSC demonstrated in vitro, summarize preclinical and clinical evidence regarding MSC safety and efficacy in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) murine model and in MS, and discuss key challenges hindering clinical translation. MSC display combined immunomodulatory and neuroprotective properties that are particularly relevant in MS. They induce sustained immune reprogramming of T cells, B cells, and myeloid cells, through paracrine signaling, extracellular vesicle release, metabolic modulation, and efferocytosis of apoptotic cells. These effects are influenced by the local microenvironment, MSC tissue source, manufacturing processes, and route of administration. Beyond immune regulation, MSC promote CNS repair by secreting neurotrophic and angiogenic factors and through mitochondrial transfer. In chronic EAE models, MSC consistently reduce disease severity, mitigate CNS inflammation, and promote neuroprotection, with enhanced efficacy following intrathecal or intraventricular administration. Early-phase clinical trials in PMS have demonstrated a favorable safety profile but inconsistent efficacy, likely reflecting substantial heterogeneity in study design, cell products, dosing regimens, and administration routes. Nevertheless, emerging evidence suggests that repeated intrathecal administration and improved patient stratification may optimize therapeutic outcomes. MSC-based therapies represent a potentially valuable avenue for PMS. However, their clinical benefit remains to be firmly established, pending well-designed trials addressing product standardization, optimized delivery approaches, and the use of robust, clinically meaningful endpoints.

title: Brain-body allometric decoupling and degree of sociality in wasps: a phylogenetic view.
abstract: The social brain hypothesis, first proposed for primates and then expanded to other vertebrates, proposes that the transition from solitary to social life was accompanied by a brain enlargement to handle new social challenges. In contrast to vertebrates, solitary insects often present larger brains than closely related eusocial species. This is attributed to the emergence of task specialization in insect societies, which may reduce the individual's behavioral repertoire and neural tissue investment. However, phylogenetic studies on how brain complexity and social behavior coevolved in insects remain scarce. Some previous studies link greater brain volume to increased social challenges faced by certain individuals in the colony, but this does not apply to all eusocial societies. Here we investigate the relationships between social evolution and brain complexity in Vespidae wasps, emphasizing the Epiponini species and their worker-controlled colonies, using volumetric data based on a phylogenetic approach. We measured brain neuropil volumes in species with varying sociality levels (solitary, primitively eusocial, and advanced eusocial) and then mapped allometric relationships and caste differences onto a Vespidae phylogenetic tree. Our findings show that the transition to eusociality was accompanied by brain-body allometric decoupling depending on caste and lineage. Queens generally exhibit greater investment in mushroom bodies, but this difference is lost in more derived Epiponini lineages. We conclude that advanced eusociality relaxes brain-body allometric constraints, thereby promoting concerted evolution among brain regions independent of body size, especially in lineages with greater caste transition flexibility, potentially facilitating whole brain volumetric changes during caste transitions.

title: Optimal timing of the General Movement Assessment for early detection of cerebral palsy.
abstract: To identify trajectories of normal fidgety movements between 10 weeks and 20 weeks corrected age and determine the optimal timing of the General Movement Assessment (GMA) to improve early cerebral palsy detection. In this prospective multicenter cohort study, parents submitted up to six serial home videos (median five per infant) between 10 weeks and 20 weeks corrected age using the Baby Moves smartphone application. GMA was performed by certified raters masked to age and clinical history. Group-based trajectory modelling identified patterns of normal fidgety movement expression over time. A total of 438 infants (233 males, 205 females) contributed 2075 videos. Four trajectories were identified: consistent fidgety (22%), later fade (63%), later onset (10%), and low prevalence (5%). The greatest overlap in normal fidgety movements occurred at 14 to 15+6 weeks corrected age. Approximately 10% of infants (later onset) demonstrated emergence of normal fidgety movements after the currently recommended initial assessment window. The low prevalence trajectory was associated with lower gestational age and greater neonatal morbidity.
