Timing influences fidgety movement classification and may affect early cerebral palsy detection. Assessment at 14 to 15+6 weeks corrected age may reduce early misclassification.

title: Computation or Weight Adaptation? Rethinking the Role of Plasticity in Learning.
abstract: The human brain is an adaptive learning system that can generalize to new tasks and unfamiliar environments. The traditional view is that such adaptive behavior requires a structural change of the learning system (e.g., via neural plasticity). In this work, we use artificial neural networks, specifically large language models (LLMs), to challenge this traditional view and suggest that such adaptive behavior can be also achieved solely through computation if the learning system is sufficiently trained. We focus on statistical learning paradigms. These require identifying underlying regularities in seemingly arbitrary word sequences and are primarily considered to require neural plasticity. LLMs can capture arbitrary structures without requiring weight adaptation, even though these structures carry no semantic content and lie far from the natural language distribution on which the models were trained. Our work provides novel insights into the role of plasticity in learning, demonstrating that sufficiently trained learning systems are highly flexible, adapting to new tasks and environments solely through computation, much more than previously acknowledged. Furthermore, our work opens the door for future research to use deep learning models to conjure hypotheses about the brain.

µ-QuEChERS as a Clean-Up Strategy for Determination of Ketamine, Cocaine, and Metabolites in Hair Samples.
abstract: The Quick, Easy, Cheap, Effective, Rugged, and Safe (QuEChERS) method is the established approach for pesticide residue analysis in Europe and possesses the qualities required for routine application across diverse analytical fields. In forensic toxicology, the analysis often involves limited sample amounts while demanding high sensitivity to support legal proceedings. Therefore, miniaturizing a versatile and rapid method such as QuEChERS can offer a greener and more efficient alternative for routine forensic laboratories. This chapter presents two µ-QuEChERS methodologies as clean-up procedures for the determination of ketamine and norketamine, and cocaine and its metabolites, in hair samples, followed by analysis using gas chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (GC-MS/MS). Both methods achieved the cut-off values recommended by the Society of Hair Testing (SoHT).

title: Analysis of Ketamine, Its Metabolites, and Analogs in Urine by DLLME and LC-MS/MS.
abstract: This chapter presents a sensitive and efficient method for the determination of ketamine, its primary metabolites (norketamine and 6-hydroxynorketamine), and its analogs 2-fluorodeschloroketamine (2F-DCK) and deschloroketamine (DCK) in urine samples. The procedure is based on dispersive liquid-liquid microextraction (DLLME) followed by LC-MS/MS detection, offering several advantages aligned with Green Analytical Toxicology principles, such as reduced solvent consumption, low sample volume, and short processing time. The method demonstrated good linearity and sensitivity and was successfully applied to authentic urine samples as a proof of concept, confirming its suitability for forensic and clinical toxicological investigations.

title: Routine LC-MS/MS Screening for Cocaine and Opiates in Whole Blood.
abstract: This study describes a method for the analysis of cocaine, its metabolites, and opioids in whole blood samples using protein precipitation, followed by detection with liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). This method utilizes low sample volumes (0.1 mL) and minimizes matrix effects for enhanced sensitivity and reproducibility. Samples are prepared straightforwardly, ensuring a reliable and fast workflow for forensic toxicological applications.

title: Simultaneous Determination of THC, THCOH, and THCCOOH in Blood and Urine by GC-MS with Microwave-Assisted Derivatization.
abstract: A sensitive and rapid method for the simultaneous determination of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), its hydroxylated metabolite (THCOH), and its carboxylated metabolite (THCCOOH) in whole blood and urine has been developed using solid-phase extraction (SPE) followed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). A microwave-assisted derivatization step was implemented to enhance analyte volatility and chromatographic performance, thereby improving detection sensitivity and reducing overall analysis time compared with conventional heating techniques. In this methodology, sample preparation is carried out by applying SPE to efficiently isolate the target cannabinoids from blood and urine matrices. Subsequent derivatization under microwave irradiation ensured complete conversion of the analytes to their more volatile derivatives, optimizing their separation and detection by GC-MS. The simplicity of the presented protocol, combined with the use of instrumentation accessible to most forensic toxicology laboratories, justifies its adoption in routine analyses.

title: Simultaneous Quantification of Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol, 11-Hydroxy-Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol, and 11-Nor-9-Carboxy-Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol in Human Urine by Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS) Following Tandem Enzyme-Alkaline Hydrolysis and Solid-Phase Extraction.
abstract: Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is the principal psychoactive cannabinoid in cannabis. Following consumption, it is metabolized in the liver to 11-hydroxy-Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol, and subsequently to 11-nor-9-carboxy-Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol, which are excreted in urine. The presence of THC and its metabolites in urine can serve as indicators of recent or past cannabis use. Here, a routine method for the simultaneous quantification of these three compounds is presented, using tandem enzymatic-alkaline hydrolysis, solid-phase extraction, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). The procedure is optimized for operational efficiency and analytical sensitivity and is routinely applied to urine samples submitted for cannabinoid testing in clinical and forensic toxicology.

title: Advanced Diffusion MRI in the Human Brain: Microstructure Imaging and Structural Connectivity.
abstract: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) is one of the most powerful MRI techniques for exploring the brain's microstructure in vivo. By measuring how water molecules move within tissue, it provides unique insight into the cellular and fiber architecture of the brain-information that conventional MRI cannot reveal. In clinical settings, diffusion imaging is now a valuable tool for early stroke diagnosis, tumour characterization, and surgical planning. In research, it enables the study of brain development, ageing, and disease progression, linking imaging findings to cellular and molecular processes. Over the past three decades, diffusion MRI has evolved from simple diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps to advanced models that capture the complexity of tissue organization. Techniques such as diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), diffusional kurtosis imaging (DKI), and multi-compartment biophysical models now allow estimation of parameters related to axonal density, myelination, and water exchange between cellular compartments. Combined with tractography, these methods enable noninvasive reconstruction of white-matter pathways and network-level connectivity, transforming dMRI into a central tool for both neuroscience and clinical use. This chapter introduces the principles and applications of diffusion MRI in a progressive manner. We begin with the fundamental physics of diffusion contrast and its clinical relevance, then move to advanced microstructural models that provide richer biological specificity. Subsequent sections describe tractography methods used to map brain connectivity and analyze structural networks. Together, these sections aim to provide readers, especially those with limited imaging background, with an accessible understanding of how diffusion MRI reveals the brain's hidden microstructure and connects it to biological function.

title: Isolation of Oligodendrogial Nuclear RNA from Fresh Frozen Human Brains for Transcriptomic Analysis.
abstract: Isolation of cell-type-specific RNA from human post-mortem brain tissue is essential for understanding gene regulatory mechanisms underlying normal brain function and neurological disease. However, dissociation of intact cells from frozen brain tissue is technically challenging and often incompatible with archived human samples. Isolation of nuclei provides a robust alternative that preserves nuclear RNA and enables transcriptomic analyses from fresh frozen tissue. Here, we describe a protocol for the isolation of oligodendrocyte lineage-enriched nuclear RNA from fresh frozen human brain tissue. Nuclei are obtained by mechanical homogenization, immunolabeled with antibodies against Olig2 and NeuN, and sorted by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). RNA is subsequently extracted from sorted nuclei for downstream molecular analyses. This approach enables reliable enrichment of oligodendroglial nuclei while excluding neuronal populations and is suitable for bulk transcriptomic applications using human brain tissue.
